problem_statement:
An Olympic diver of mass m begins a descent from a diving board of height h=10\unit{m} with zero initial velocity. Take gravitational acceleration g=9.8\unit{m/s^2}. After entering the water, assume the buoyant force balances the diver's weight so the net gravitational-buoyant force is zero, and the only retarding force is a viscous drag F_d=b v^2 acting upward, where b is a positive constant and v is the downward speed. Let x denote the vertical depth below the water surface measured downward with x=0 at the surface. Let t denote time measured from the instant of impact with the water, so t=0 at x=0. Let T denote the elapsed time in air from the dive until impact. Let V_0 be the speed on impact with the water (at x=0). Let V(x) denote the speed at depth x under water, with V(x)=\frac{dx}{dt} for t>0.

a) Calculate the velocity V_0 on impact with the water and the approximate elapsed time T from the dive until impact. Use any method you choose.

b) Set up the equation of motion for vertical descent of the diver through the water. Solve for the velocity V(x) as a function of the depth x under water and impose the boundary condition V(0)=V_0.

c) If b/m=\frac{2}{5}\unit{m^{-1}}, estimate the depth x at which V(x)=\frac{V_0}{10}.

d) Solve for the vertical depth x(t) of the diver under water in terms of the time t under water, with x=0 at t=0.
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 $$V_0=\sqrt{2 g h}$$
$$V_0=\sqrt{2\cdot 9.8\cdot 10}$$
$$V_0=14\unit{m/s}$$
$$T=\frac{V_0}{g}$$
$$T=1.43\unit{s}$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 $$m\frac{d^2 x}{dt^2}=-b\Big(\frac{dx}{dt}\Big)^2$$
$$V(x)=\frac{dx}{dt}$$
$$m V\frac{dV}{dx}=-b V^2$$
$$\frac{dV}{V}=-\frac{b}{m} dx$$
$$\int_{V_0}^{V(x)} \frac{dV}{V}=-\frac{b}{m} \int_0^x dx$$
$$\ln\frac{V(x)}{V_0}=-\frac{b}{m} x$$
$$V(x)=V_0 e^{-\frac{b}{m} x}$$

Solution for subproblem(c):
 $$\frac{b}{m}=\frac{2}{5}\unit{m^{-1}}$$
$$V(x)=\frac{V_0}{10}$$
$$x=\frac{m}{b} \ln 10$$
$$x=\frac{5}{2} \ln 10\unit{m}$$
$$x=5.76\unit{m}$$

Solution for subproblem(d):
 $$\frac{dx}{dt}=V_0 e^{-\frac{b}{m} x}$$
$$e^{\frac{b}{m} x} dx=V_0 dt$$
$$\int_0^x e^{\frac{b}{m} u} du=V_0 \int_0^t dt$$
$$\frac{m}{b} \big( e^{\frac{b}{m} x}-1 \big)=V_0 t$$
$$x=\frac{m}{b} \ln\big(1+\frac{b V_0 t}{m}\big)$$
model_response:
### a) Motion through air

Taking downward as positive,

$$
V_0^2=2gh
$$

$$
V_0=\sqrt{2gh}
$$

$$
V_0=\sqrt{2(9.8\unit{m/s^2})(10\unit{m})}
$$

$$
\boxed{V_0=14\unit{m/s}}
$$

The elapsed time satisfies

$$
h=\frac{1}{2}gT^2
$$

$$
T=\sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}
$$

$$
\boxed{T\approx1.43\unit{s}}
$$

### b) Velocity as a function of depth

The upward drag force gives

$$
m\frac{dV}{dt}=-bV^2
$$

Using $V=\frac{dx}{dt}$,

$$
\frac{dV}{dt}=V\frac{dV}{dx}
$$

$$
mV\frac{dV}{dx}=-bV^2
$$

$$
\frac{dV}{V}=-\frac{b}{m}dx
$$

Applying $V(0)=V_0$,

$$
\int_{V_0}^{V(x)}\frac{dV}{V}=-\frac{b}{m}\int_0^x dx
$$

$$
\ln\frac{V(x)}{V_0}=-\frac{b}{m}x
$$

$$
\boxed{V(x)=V_0e^{-bx/m}}
$$

### c) Depth at one-tenth the impact speed

$$
\frac{V_0}{10}=V_0e^{-bx/m}
$$

$$
x=\frac{m}{b}\ln 10
$$

Given $\frac{b}{m}=\frac{2}{5}\unit{m^{-1}}$,

$$
\frac{m}{b}=\frac{5}{2}\unit{m}
$$

$$
\boxed{x\approx5.76\unit{m}}
$$

### d) Depth as a function of underwater time

$$
\frac{dx}{dt}=V_0e^{-bx/m}
$$

$$
e^{bx/m}dx=V_0dt
$$

Applying $x(0)=0$,

$$
\int_0^{x(t)}e^{bx/m}dx=V_0\int_0^t dt
$$

$$
\frac{m}{b}\left(e^{bx/m}-1\right)=V_0t
$$

$$
e^{bx/m}=1+\frac{bV_0}{m}t
$$

$$
\boxed{x(t)=\frac{m}{b}\ln\left(1+\frac{bV_0}{m}t\right)}
$$

It also correctly obtains $V_0=\sqrt{2gh}=14\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and $T=\sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}=\frac{V_0}{g}\approx1.43\,\mathrm{s}$.

problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) Consider circular orbits just above the surfaces of Earth and Moon. A near-Earth satellite completes one revolution in about 90 \unit{min}, and a satellite orbiting just above the Moon’s surface also completes one revolution in about 90 \unit{min}. Let m be the mass of the satellite, r the orbital radius measured from the center of the central body, M the mass of the central body, \omega the orbital angular speed, T the orbital period, and G the gravitational constant. Let M_e and M_m be the masses of Earth and Moon, R_e and R_m their radii, V_e and V_m their volumes, and \rho_e and \rho_m their mean densities. What interesting statement can you derive about the Moon’s composition? State the conclusion as an equation involving \rho_e and \rho_m.
reference_solution:
From the orbital condition for uniform circular motion under gravitation

$$
m r \omega^2 = \frac{G m M}{r^2}
$$

we obtain

$$
r^3 \omega^2 = G M
$$

Using the relation between period and angular speed

$$
T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega}
$$

equal periods for near-surface Earth and Moon orbits imply equal angular speeds, so with r_e = R_e and r_m = R_m we have

$$
\frac{r_m^3}{r_e^3} = \frac{M_m}{M_e}
$$

Since volume scales as the cube of the radius, it follows that

$$
\frac{M_e}{V_e} = \frac{M_m}{V_m}
$$

Hence the mean densities satisfy

$$
\rho_e = \rho_m
$$

Therefore, the Earth and the Moon have the same mean density, implying a similar average composition.
model_response:
### Solution

For a circular orbit, gravity provides the centripetal force:

$$
\frac{GMm}{r^2}=m\omega^2r
$$

Thus:

$$
\omega^2=\frac{GM}{r^3}
$$

Using $\omega=2\pi/T$:

$$
T^2=\frac{4\pi^2r^3}{GM}
$$

For orbits just above the surfaces, $r\approx R_e$ for Earth and $r\approx R_m$ for the Moon. Since their periods are approximately equal:

$$
\frac{R_e^3}{M_e}\approx\frac{R_m^3}{M_m}
$$

Therefore:

$$
\frac{M_e}{R_e^3}\approx\frac{M_m}{R_m^3}
$$

For a spherical body:

$$
V=\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3
$$

Using $\rho=M/V$:

$$
\rho_e=\frac{3M_e}{4\pi R_e^3}
$$

$$
\rho_m=\frac{3M_m}{4\pi R_m^3}
$$

### Final Answer

The Moon’s mean composition has approximately the same density as Earth’s mean composition:

$$
\boxed{\rho_m\approx\rho_e}
$$

problem_statement:
A particle of mass m moves under the influence of an attractive central force f(r) directed toward the origin. Let r be the radial distance from the origin. Define the potential V(r) by f(r) = - dV/dr. Let J be the conserved magnitude of the particle's angular momentum. Define the effective potential V^*(r) = J^2/(2 m r^2) + V(r). Let E be the total mechanical energy. A circular orbit at radius r_0 is one for which the radial motion is stationary at r = r_0, and it may be subjected to a small radial perturbation about r_0.

a) Show that by a proper choice of initial conditions a circular orbit can result. The circular orbit is now subjected to a small radial perturbation.

b) Determine the relation that must hold among f(r), r, and \partial f/\partial r for this circular orbit to be stable. Now assume that the force law is of the form f(r) = -K/r^n with K>0.

c) Determine the maximum value of n for which the circular orbit can be stable.
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 The effective potential is
$$V^*(r)=\frac{J^2}{2 m r^2}+V(r)$$
Here J is the conserved angular momentum and V(r) is related to the central force by
$$f(r)=-\frac{dV}{dr}$$
In terms of these, the total energy is
$$E=\frac{m \dot r^2}{2}+V^*(r)$$
Thus the radial motion is equivalent to one-dimensional motion in V^*(r). A circular orbit at radius r_0 corresponds to an equilibrium point where
$$\frac{dV^*}{dr}=0$$
which implies
$$\frac{dV}{dr}=\frac{J^2}{m r^3}$$
evaluated at r=r_0. If the initial conditions satisfy these and
$$E=V^*(r_0)$$
then the orbit is circular

Solution for subproblem(b):
 For the orbit to be stable, V^*(r) must have a minimum at r=r_0, which requires
$$\frac{d^2 V^*}{dr^2}>0$$
Equivalently,
$$\frac{3 J^2}{m r^4}+\frac{d^2 V}{dr^2}>0$$
Using f(r)=-dV/dr, this becomes
$$\frac{3 J^2}{m r^4}-\frac{df}{dr}>0$$
evaluated at r=r_0

Solution for subproblem(c):
 For f(r)=-\frac{K}{r^n} with K>0,
$$\frac{df}{dr}=\frac{n K}{r^{n+1}}$$
At the circular-orbit radius r_0, the equilibrium condition gives
$$J^2=\frac{m K}{r_0^{n-3}}$$
The stability requirement is
$$\frac{3 J^2}{m r^4}-\frac{df}{dr}>0$$
Using the force law in this inequality yields
$$\frac{3 K}{r^{n+1}}-\frac{n K}{r^{n+1}}>0$$
which requires
$$n<3$$
for the circular orbit to be stable
model_response:
### a) Circular orbit

The radial energy equation is

$$
E=\frac{1}{2}m\dot r^2+V^*(r)
$$

A circular orbit at $r=r_0$ requires

$$
\dot r_0=0
$$

$$
\frac{dV^*}{dr}\bigg|_{r_0}=0
$$

Since

$$
\frac{dV^*}{dr}=-\frac{J^2}{mr^3}-f(r)
$$

the required force balance is

$$
f(r_0)=-\frac{J^2}{mr_0^3}
$$

Thus choose the initial conditions

$$
r(0)=r_0
$$

$$
\dot r(0)=0
$$

$$
E=V^*(r_0)
$$

with $J$ satisfying the force-balance condition above

### b) Stability condition

For a small radial perturbation, stability requires a local minimum of $V^*(r)$

$$
\frac{d^2V^*}{dr^2}\bigg|_{r_0}>0
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{d^2V^*}{dr^2}=\frac{3J^2}{mr^4}-\frac{\partial f}{\partial r}
$$

Using the circular-orbit condition,

$$
\frac{J^2}{mr_0^3}=-f(r_0)
$$

Therefore,

$$
-\frac{3f(r_0)}{r_0}-\frac{\partial f}{\partial r}\bigg|_{r_0}>0
$$

Equivalently, the stability condition is

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial r}\bigg|_{r_0}+\frac{3f(r_0)}{r_0}<0
$$

### c) Power-law force

For

$$
f(r)=-\frac{K}{r^n}
$$

the radial derivative is

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial r}=\frac{nK}{r^{n+1}}
$$

Substitution into the stability condition gives

$$
\frac{nK}{r_0^{n+1}}-\frac{3K}{r_0^{n+1}}<0
$$

Since $K>0$ and $r_0>0$,

$$
n<3
$$

Thus the limiting value is

$$
n_{\max}=3
$$

The orbit is strictly stable only for $n<3$; $n=3$ is marginally stable rather than strictly stable

AI_audit.reason: The model’s equations are physically and algebraically equivalent to the valid reference: circular balance gives f(r_0)=-J^2/(m r_0^3), and V^{*\prime\prime}(r_0)>0 gives f'(r_0)+3f(r_0)/r_0<0. For f=-K/r^n this reduces to (n-3)K/r_0^{n+1}<0, hence strict stability requires n<3; the model also correctly identifies n=3 as the marginal limiting exponent.

problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) Consider a planet of mass m moving in a nearly circular orbit of radius R around a star of mass M. Let r be the star–planet separation and θ the true anomaly. In addition to Newtonian gravitation, the planet experiences a central repulsive force proportional to r with constant A > 0, directed outward. Let G denote Newton's gravitational constant. Let F_r denote the total radial force on the planet. Define u = 1/r. Let h be the specific angular momentum defined by h = r^2 dθ/dt, where t is time. A dot over a symbol denotes a time derivative d/dt. The periastron is the point of closest approach. Let θ_1 and θ_2 be the true anomalies at two successive periastrons. Define Δθ = θ_2 − θ_1 as the angular advance between successive periastrons, Δθ_p as the precession per revolution, Δt as the time for this precession, and ω_p as its angular velocity. Let u_0 denote the constant value of u for the exactly circular orbit, and let δu be a small perturbation about u_0. Let B be a constant oscillation amplitude and a a dimensionless frequency factor defined in the solution. Compute ω_p.
reference_solution:
The total radial force on the planet is
$$
F_r = - \frac{G M m}{r^2} + A r
$$
Using u = 1/r and Binet's formula, the orbit equation is
$$
- m h^2 u^2 \frac{d^2 u}{d\theta^2} - m h^2 u^3 = - G M m u^2 + \frac{A}{u}
$$
For a nearly circular orbit, write
$$
\nu = u_0 + \delta u
$$
Substituting and keeping terms to first order in \delta u gives
$$
 m h^2 \frac{d^2 (\delta u)}{d\theta^2} + m h^2 u_0 + m h^2 \delta u = G M m - \frac{A}{u_0^3 \left( 1 - \frac{\delta u}{u_0} \right)^3}
$$
To first order in \delta u,
$$
 m h^2 \frac{d^2 (\delta u)}{d\theta^2} + m h^2 u_0 + m h^2 \delta u \approx G M m - \frac{A}{u_0^3} + \frac{3 A}{u_0^4} \delta u
$$
For an exactly circular orbit,
$$
\delta u = 0
$$
and
$$\nu = u_0
$$
The circular-orbit condition is
$$
 m h^2 u_0 = G M m - \frac{A}{u_0^3}
$$
Using this in the perturbed equation yields
$$
 m h^2 \frac{d^2 (\delta u)}{d\theta^2} + m h^2 \delta u = \frac{3 A}{u_0^4} \delta u
$$
Therefore,
$$
 \frac{d^2 (\delta u)}{d\theta^2} + \left( 1 - \frac{3 A}{m h^2 u_0^4} \right) \delta u = 0
$$
Choosing axes so that the solution is sinusoidal,
$$
 \delta u = B \sin(a \theta)
$$
The parameter a is
$$
 a = \sqrt{1 - \frac{3 A}{m h^2 u_0^4}}
$$
Relating to the circular orbit radius,
$$
 u_0 = \frac{1}{R}
$$
From the circular-orbit condition,
$$
 m h^2 u_0^4 = G M m u_0^3 - A
$$
Hence,
$$
 a = \sqrt{1 - \frac{3 A}{G M m u_0^3 - A}}
$$
Substituting u_0 = 1/R,
$$
 a = \sqrt{1 - \frac{3 A R^3}{G M m - A R^3}}
$$
For two successive periastrons,
$$
 a \theta_2 - a \theta_1 = 2 \pi
$$
Define
$$
 \Delta \theta = \theta_2 - \theta_1
$$
Then
$$
 a \Delta \theta = 2 \pi
$$
Thus,
$$
 \Delta \theta = \frac{2 \pi}{a}
$$
The periastron precession per revolution is
$$
 \Delta \theta_p = \Delta \theta - 2 \pi
$$
Therefore,
$$
 \Delta \theta_p = \frac{2 \pi (1 - a)}{a}
$$
The time for this precession is
$$
 \Delta t = \frac{\Delta \theta}{\dot{\theta}}
$$
Hence,
$$
 \Delta t = \frac{2 \pi}{a \dot{\theta}}
$$
The angular velocity of precession is
$$
 \omega_p = \frac{\Delta \theta_p}{\Delta t}
$$
Therefore,
$$
 \omega_p = (1 - a) \dot{\theta}
$$
From the definition of h,
$$
 h = r^2 \frac{d\theta}{dt}
$$
At r = R,
$$
 \dot{\theta} = \frac{h}{R^2}
$$
Using the circular-orbit condition,
$$
 \dot{\theta} = \sqrt{\frac{G M}{R^3} - \frac{A}{m}}
$$
Moreover,
$$
 a \dot{\theta} = \sqrt{\frac{G M}{R^3} - \frac{4 A}{m}}
$$
Therefore,
$$
 \omega_p = \sqrt{\frac{G M}{R^3} - \frac{A}{m}} - \sqrt{\frac{G M}{R^3} - \frac{4 A}{m}}
$$
model_response:
### Radial force

Taking outward as positive,

$$
F_r=-\frac{GMm}{r^2}+Ar
$$

With $u=1/r$, Binet’s equation is

$$
\frac{d^2u}{d\theta^2}+u=-\frac{F_r}{mh^2u^2}
$$

Hence

$$
\frac{d^2u}{d\theta^2}+u=\frac{GM}{h^2}-\frac{A}{mh^2u^3}
$$

### Nearly circular orbit

Let

$$
u=u_0+\delta u
$$

For the circular orbit,

$$
u_0=\frac{GM}{h^2}-\frac{A}{mh^2u_0^3}
$$

Linearizing in $\delta u$ gives

$$
\frac{d^2\delta u}{d\theta^2}+a^2\delta u=0
$$

where

$$
a^2=1-\frac{3A}{mh^2u_0^4}
$$

Thus

$$
\delta u=B\cos(a\theta)
$$

Successive periastrons are separated by

$$
\Delta\theta=\frac{2\pi}{a}
$$

The precession per revolution is

$$
\Delta\theta_p=2\pi\left(\frac{1}{a}-1\right)
$$

Since $\dot{\theta}=h/R^2$, the time between successive periastrons is

$$
\Delta t=\frac{2\pi R^2}{ah}
$$

Therefore

$$
\omega_p=\frac{\Delta\theta_p}{\Delta t}
$$

$$
\omega_p=\frac{h}{R^2}(1-a)
$$

For the circular orbit, radial force balance gives

$$
\frac{h^2}{R^3}=\frac{GM}{R^2}-\frac{AR}{m}
$$

Thus

$$
\frac{h}{R^2}=\sqrt{\frac{GM}{R^3}-\frac{A}{m}}
$$

Also,

$$
a=\sqrt{\frac{\frac{GM}{R^3}-\frac{4A}{m}}{\frac{GM}{R^3}-\frac{A}{m}}}
$$

### Final answer

$$
\boxed{\omega_p=\sqrt{\frac{GM}{R^3}-\frac{A}{m}}-\sqrt{\frac{GM}{R^3}-\frac{4A}{m}}}
$$

For weak repulsion,

$$
\boxed{\omega_p\approx\frac{3A}{2m}\sqrt{\frac{R^3}{GM}}}
$$

AI_audit.reason: The model’s result exactly matches the valid reference. Circular balance gives $Ω^2=GM/R^3−A/m$, while linear radial perturbations give the epicyclic frequency $κ^2=GM/R^3−4A/m$; hence the apsidal precession rate is $ω_p=Ω−κ$, equal to the boxed expression. This applies to the implicitly required stable nearly circular regime $GM/R^3>4A/m$.

reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 Let M and R be the Moon's mass and radius, respectively, and let m be the mass of a test body at the surface. By Newton's law of gravitation, the gravitational force equals m g at the surface.
$$\frac{G M m}{R^{2}} = m g$$
Solving for g gives
$$g = \frac{G M}{R^{2}}$$
With the given data
$$G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\unit{m^3/(kg s^2)}$$
$$M = 7.35\times 10^{22}\unit{kg}$$
$$R = 1.74\times 10^{6}\unit{m}$$
Substituting yields
$$g = 1.62\unit{m/s^2}$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 The gravitational potential energy at radial distance ρ from the Moon's center is
$$U(\rho) = -\frac{G M m}{\rho}$$
Using g = G M / R^{2}, this can also be written as
$$U(\rho) = -\frac{m g R^{2}}{\rho}$$
To escape to infinity (ρ → ∞), the minimum total energy is zero. At the surface (ρ = R), the total energy is
$$E = \frac{1}{2} m v_{0}^{2} - m g R$$
For escape, set
$$E = 0$$
Solving for the escape velocity gives
$$v_{0} = \sqrt{2 g R}$$
Using the numerical values g and R from part (a), we have
$$v_{0} = \sqrt{2 \times 1.62 \times 1.74 \times 10^{6}}$$
Therefore
$$v_{0} = 2.37\times 10^{3}\unit{m/s}$$
model_response:
### a) Gravitational acceleration

Newton’s gravitational force at the surface is

$$
F=\frac{GMm}{R^2}
$$

Using $F=mg$

$$
mg=\frac{GMm}{R^2}
$$

Therefore

$$
g=\frac{GM}{R^2}
$$

Substitution gives

$$
g=\frac{(6.67\times10^{-11})(7.35\times10^{22})}{(1.74\times10^6)^2}\unit{m/s^2}
$$

$$
g=1.62\unit{m/s^2}
$$

### b) Escape velocity

The gravitational potential energy at radial distance $\rho$ is

$$
U(\rho)=-\frac{GMm}{\rho}
$$

At the Moon’s surface

$$
U(R)=-\frac{GMm}{R}
$$

For minimum escape velocity, the total mechanical energy is zero

$$
E=\frac{1}{2}mv_0^2-\frac{GMm}{R}
$$

$$
E=0
$$

Thus

$$
\frac{1}{2}mv_0^2=\frac{GMm}{R}
$$

$$
v_0=\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}}
$$

Substitution gives

$$
v_0=\sqrt{\frac{2(6.67\times10^{-11})(7.35\times10^{22})}{1.74\times10^6}}\unit{m/s}
$$

$$
v_0=2.37\times10^3\unit{m/s}
$$

### Final answer

$$
g=1.62\unit{m/s^2}
$$

$$
v_0=2.37\times10^3\unit{m/s}
$$

AI_audit.reason: The model response matches the valid reference both symbolically and numerically: $g=GM/R^2=1.62\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ and, from $(1/2)mv_0^2-GMm/R=0$, $v_0=\sqrt{2GM/R}=\sqrt{2gR}=2.37\times 10^3\ \mathrm{m/s}$. There is no substantive physics or algebra error.

problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) A perfectly smooth horizontal disk rotates with constant angular velocity ω about a vertical axis through its center O. A person standing on the disk at radial distance R from O pushes a perfectly smooth coin (negligible size) of mass m directly toward O, imparting to it an initial speed V relative to the disk. Consider the motion as observed in the rotating frame rigidly attached to the disk. Let a right-handed Cartesian frame (x, y, z) be fixed in the disk with the z-axis along the rotation axis, the x-axis chosen opposite to the initial velocity of the coin, and the y-axis completing the right-handed triad. Let r be the position vector and v the velocity in this rotating frame. Let k be the unit vector along +z. Let i denote the imaginary unit used later for a complex representation in the disk plane. Over a short time interval 0 ≤ t ≤ Ψ_t during which (ω t)^2 is negligible, show that the trajectory seen by the person on the disk is approximately a parabola and give its equation in the form y = f(x).
reference_solution:
In a rotating frame, the planar motion of the coin satisfies
$$
m \frac{d\bf v}{dt} = \bf F - m \frac{d\boldsymbol{\omega}}{dt} \times \bf r - m \boldsymbol{\omega} \times (\boldsymbol{\omega} \times \bf r) - 2 m \boldsymbol{\omega} \times \bf v
$$
After the initial push there is no horizontal force on the coin, and the disk rotates with constant angular velocity
$$
\boldsymbol{\omega} = \omega \bf k
$$
so that
$$
\frac{d\boldsymbol{\omega}}{dt} = 0
$$
Therefore the in-plane components obey
$$
\ddot x = \omega^2 x + 2 \omega \dot y
$$
$$
\ddot y = \omega^2 y - 2 \omega \dot x
$$
Introduce the complex variable
$$
z = x + i y
$$
Then
$$
\ddot z + 2 i \omega \dot z - \omega^2 z = 0
$$
Seek a solution of the form
$$
z = e^{\gamma t}
$$
which yields the characteristic equation
$$
\gamma^2 + 2 i \omega \gamma - \omega^2 = 0
$$
Equivalently
$$
(\gamma + i \omega)^2 = 0
$$
Thus the double root is
$$
\gamma = - i \omega
$$
The general solution is
$$
z = (A + i B) e^{- i \omega t} + (C + i D) t e^{- i \omega t}
$$
The initial conditions at t = 0 are
$$
x(0) = R
$$
$$
y(0) = 0
$$
$$
\dot x(0) = - V
$$
$$
\dot y(0) = 0
$$
which are equivalently
$$
z(0) = R
$$
$$
\dot z(0) = - V
$$
These give
$$
R = A + i B
$$
$$
- V = \omega B + C + i (D - \omega A)
$$
so that
$$
A = R
$$
$$
B = 0
$$
$$
C = - V
$$
$$
D = \omega R
$$
Hence
$$
z = \big( (R - V t) + i R \omega t \big) e^{- i \omega t}
$$
Extracting real and imaginary parts gives
$$
x = (R - V t) \cos(\omega t) + R \omega t \sin(\omega t)
$$
$$
y = - (R - V t) \sin(\omega t) + R \omega t \cos(\omega t)
$$
For times such that (\omega t)^2 is negligible, use
$$
\sin(\omega t) \approx \omega t
$$
$$
\cos(\omega t) \approx 1
$$
which yields
$$
x \approx R - V t
$$
$$
y \approx V \omega t^2
$$
Eliminating t using t = (R - x) \slash V gives the approximate trajectory in the rotating frame as the parabola
$$
y = \frac{\omega}{V} (R - x)^2

### Solution

In the rotating frame, the coin experiences Coriolis and centrifugal accelerations

$$
\frac{d^2\boldsymbol r}{dt^2}=-2\omega\boldsymbol k\times\frac{d\boldsymbol r}{dt}+\omega^2\boldsymbol r
$$

Thus

$$
\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}=2\omega\frac{dy}{dt}+\omega^2x
$$

$$
\frac{d^2y}{dt^2}=-2\omega\frac{dx}{dt}+\omega^2y
$$

The initial conditions are

$$
x(0)=R
$$

$$
y(0)=0
$$

$$
\frac{dx}{dt}(0)=-V
$$

$$
\frac{dy}{dt}(0)=0
$$

Introduce the complex coordinate $q=x+iy$

$$
\frac{d^2q}{dt^2}+2i\omega\frac{dq}{dt}-\omega^2q=0
$$

Its exact solution satisfying the initial conditions is

$$
q=[R+(-V+i\omega R)t]e^{-i\omega t}
$$

For $(\omega t)^2\ll1$

$$
e^{-i\omega t}\approx1-i\omega t
$$

Neglecting terms of order $(\omega t)^2$

$$
q\approx R-Vt+i\omega Vt^2
$$

Therefore

$$
x\approx R-Vt
$$

$$
y\approx\omega Vt^2
$$

Eliminating $t$

$$
t\approx\frac{R-x}{V}
$$

### Final answer

$$
\boxed{y=\frac{\omega}{V}(R-x)^2}
$$

Hence, for $0\leq t\leq\Psi_t$ with $(\omega\Psi_t)^2\ll1$, the trajectory observed from the rotating disk is approximately a parabola with vertex at $(R,0)$ opening toward positive $y$.

problem_statement:
Consider a classical system of point masses m_i with position vectors r_i(t) in three-dimensional space. Each mass experiences a net applied force F_i(r_i,t). A dot over a symbol denotes a time derivative, and a centered dot denotes the Euclidean dot product between vectors. The total kinetic energy of the system is denoted by T. The time average of any time-dependent quantity A(t) over an interval of length τ is defined below. For periodic motion take τ to be the common period; otherwise consider the limit τ → ∞. In part (b), consider a single particle with position vector r(t), radial distance r = |r(t)|, potential energy V(r), and a constant C such that V(r) = C/r describes a central inverse-square law potential. The net force on the particle is F(t)

a) Consider the quantity below, assumed to remain finite at all times, and prove the virial theorem shown afterward, where the overline denotes a time average and T is the total kinetic energy of the system
$$\sum_{i} m_{i} \frac{dr_{i}}{dt} \cdot r_{i}$$
$$\overline{T} = -\frac{1}{2} \overline{\sum_{i} F_{i} \cdot r_{i}}$$

b) In the case of a single particle acted on by a central inverse-square law force, show that the time-averaged kinetic energy satisfies the relation below, where V is the potential energy
$$\overline{T} = -\frac{\overline{V}}{2}$$
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 Define Q(t) by
$$Q(t) = \sum_{i} m_{i} \frac{dr_{i}}{dt} \cdot r_{i}$$
Differentiate Q(t) with respect to time
$$\frac{dQ}{dt} = \sum_{i} m_{i} \frac{dr_{i}}{dt} \cdot \frac{dr_{i}}{dt} + \sum_{i} m_{i} \frac{d^{2} r_{i}}{dt^{2}} \cdot r_{i}$$
Use Newton's second law
$$m_{i} \frac{d^{2} r_{i}}{dt^{2}} = F_{i}$$
Substitute to obtain
$$\frac{dQ}{dt} = \sum_{i} m_{i} \frac{dr_{i}}{dt} \cdot \frac{dr_{i}}{dt} + \sum_{i} F_{i} \cdot r_{i}$$
Introduce the total kinetic energy
$$T = \sum_{i} \frac{1}{2} m_{i} \frac{dr_{i}}{dt} \cdot \frac{dr_{i}}{dt}$$
Therefore
$$\frac{dQ}{dt} = 2 T + \sum_{i} F_{i} \cdot r_{i}$$
Define the time average
$$\overline{A} = \frac{1}{\tau} \int_{0}^{\tau} A dt$$
Average dQ/dt over the interval [0, τ]
$$\overline{\frac{dQ}{dt}} = \frac{1}{\tau} \int_{0}^{\tau} \frac{dQ}{dt} dt$$
Evaluate the average of the time derivative
$$\overline{\frac{dQ}{dt}} = \frac{Q(\tau) - Q(0)}{\tau}$$
Average the right-hand side
$$\overline{\frac{dQ}{dt}} = \overline{2 T} + \overline{\sum_{i} F_{i} \cdot r_{i}}$$
For periodic motion with common period τ, or for τ \u2192 \u221e with Q(t) finite, the boundary term vanishes, hence
$$2 \overline{T} + \overline{\sum_{i} F_{i} \cdot r_{i}} = 0$$
Therefore
$$\overline{T} = -\frac{1}{2} \overline{\sum_{i} F_{i} \cdot r_{i}}$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 Choose the central inverse-square law potential
$$V(r) = \frac{C}{r}$$
The force on the particle is
$$F(t) = -
abla V(r)$$
For a spherically symmetric potential V(r), one has
$$r(t) \cdot 
abla V(r) = r \frac{dV}{dr}$$
Therefore
$$F(t) \cdot r(t) = - r \frac{dV}{dr}$$
With V(r) = C/r, compute the derivative
$$\frac{dV}{dr} = -\frac{C}{r^{2}}$$
Hence
$$F(t) \cdot r(t) = \frac{C}{r}$$
Apply the virial theorem for one particle
$$\overline{T} = -\frac{1}{2} \overline{F(t) \cdot r(t)}$$
Thus
$$\overline{T} = -\frac{1}{2} \overline{\frac{C}{r}}$$
Since V = C/r, it follows that
$$\overline{T} = -\frac{\overline{V}}{2}$$
model_response:
### a) Virial theorem

Define the virial quantity $G(t)$ and total kinetic energy $T$:

$$
G(t)=\sum_i m_i\frac{dr_i}{dt}\cdot r_i
$$

$$
T=\frac{1}{2}\sum_i m_i\frac{dr_i}{dt}\cdot\frac{dr_i}{dt}
$$

Differentiate $G(t)$:

$$
\frac{dG}{dt}=\sum_i m_i\frac{d^2r_i}{dt^2}\cdot r_i+\sum_i m_i\frac{dr_i}{dt}\cdot\frac{dr_i}{dt}
$$

Using $m_i\frac{d^2r_i}{dt^2}=F_i$:

$$
\frac{dG}{dt}=\sum_i F_i\cdot r_i+2T
$$

The time average is

$$
\overline{A}=\frac{1}{\tau}\int_0^\tau A(t)dt
$$

Therefore,

$$
\overline{\frac{dG}{dt}}=\frac{G(\tau)-G(0)}{\tau}
$$

For periodic motion, $G(\tau)=G(0)$. For bounded nonperiodic motion, the limit as $\tau\to\infty$ is zero:

$$
\overline{\frac{dG}{dt}}=0
$$

Hence,

$$
0=\overline{\sum_i F_i\cdot r_i}+2\overline{T}
$$

$$
\boxed{\overline{T}=-\frac{1}{2}\overline{\sum_i F_i\cdot r_i}}
$$

### b) Inverse-square central force

The potential energy is

$$
V(r)=\frac{C}{r}
$$

Its radial derivative is

$$
\frac{dV}{dr}=-\frac{C}{r^2}
$$

The central force is

$$
F=-\frac{dV}{dr}\frac{r}{r}
$$

Thus,

$$
F=\frac{C}{r^3}r
$$

Consequently,

$$
F\cdot r=\frac{C}{r}
$$

$$
F\cdot r=V
$$

Applying the virial theorem for one particle gives

$$
\overline{T}=-\frac{1}{2}\overline{F\cdot r}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{\overline{T}=-\frac{\overline{V}}{2}}
$$

problem_statement:
A rocket moves in deep space, far from external forces such as gravity. The rocket carries a fixed onboard energy E. Let v denote the rocket's speed in an inertial frame, w the exhaust speed relative to the rocket (which may depend on the instantaneous total mass m of the rocket), m the instantaneous total mass of the rocket, m1 the initial mass at time t=0, and m2 the final mass after the propellant is exhausted. The rocket starts from rest at t=0. Let v_max denote the maximum speed achieved when m=m2.

a) Find the maximum speed v that the ship can achieve starting from rest. E, m1, and m2 are fixed, but the exhaust velocity w (relative to the ship) may vary as a function of the instantaneous mass m of the ship.

b) What is the maximum speed v that can be obtained if the exhaust velocity w is constrained to be constant?
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 Using the variable-mass equation of motion for a rocket in free space
$$m \frac{dv}{dt} = - w(m) \frac{dm}{dt}$$
with initial conditions at t=0
$$v=0$$
$$m=m_1$$
integration gives
$$v = - \int_{m_1}^{m} \frac{w(m)}{m} dm$$
Hence the maximum speed is
$$v_{max} = - \int_{m_1}^{m_2} \frac{w(m)}{m} dm$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 For constant w, the maximum speed is
$$v_{max} = w \ln \frac{m_1}{m_2}$$
model_response:
### Step 1: Rocket equation and energy

For an infinitesimal decrease $dm<0$,

$$
dv=-\frac{w(m)}{m}dm
$$

The energy used to eject the propellant is

$$
dE=-\frac{1}{2}w^2(m)dm
$$

Thus,

$$
v_{\max}=\int_{m_2}^{m_1}\frac{w(m)}{m}dm
$$

$$
E=\frac{1}{2}\int_{m_2}^{m_1}w^2(m)dm
$$

### a) Variable exhaust speed

By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality,

$$
v_{\max}^2\leq\int_{m_2}^{m_1}w^2(m)dm\int_{m_2}^{m_1}\frac{1}{m^2}dm
$$

$$
\int_{m_2}^{m_1}w^2(m)dm=2E
$$

$$
\int_{m_2}^{m_1}\frac{1}{m^2}dm=\frac{1}{m_2}-\frac{1}{m_1}
$$

Therefore,

$$
v_{\max}^2\leq2E\left(\frac{1}{m_2}-\frac{1}{m_1}\right)
$$

Equality requires $w(m)\propto 1/m$. The optimal exhaust speed is

$$
w(m)=\frac{1}{m}\sqrt{\frac{2E}{\frac{1}{m_2}-\frac{1}{m_1}}}
$$

Hence,

$$
\boxed{v_{\max}=\sqrt{2E\left(\frac{1}{m_2}-\frac{1}{m_1}\right)}}
$$

### b) Constant exhaust speed

For constant $w$,

$$
E=\frac{1}{2}w^2(m_1-m_2)
$$

$$
w=\sqrt{\frac{2E}{m_1-m_2}}
$$

The rocket equation gives

$$
v_{\max}=w\ln\left(\frac{m_1}{m_2}\right)
$$

Thus,

$$
\boxed{v_{\max}=\sqrt{\frac{2E}{m_1-m_2}}\ln\left(\frac{m_1}{m_2}\right)}
$$

AI_audit.reason: The reference does not impose the fixed-energy constraint and therefore does not perform the requested maximization. With the standard onboard exhaust-energy relation E=(1/2)∫_{m2}^{m1}w(m)^2 dm, Cauchy–Schwarz gives v_max=sqrt[2E(1/m2−1/m1)], attained for w(m)∝1/m; for constant w, w=sqrt[2E/(m1−m2)] and v_max=w ln(m1/m2). The reference merely states the rocket-equation integral and leaves w unconstrained, so it is materially incomplete/incorrect.

problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) A uniform cube has side length 2a. The origin is at the center of mass, and the Cartesian axes x, y, z pass through the centers of the three pairs of opposite faces. Let I_{0} denote the moment of inertia about any axis through the center of mass and perpendicular to a face (equivalently, an axis through the center of mass and the center of one face). Let I_{corner} denote the moment of inertia about the axis through the center of mass and a corner (the body diagonal). Let I_{xx}, I_{yy}, I_{zz} be the moments of inertia about the x, y, z axes through the center of mass, and let I_{xy}, I_{yz}, I_{zx} be the corresponding products of inertia. For an axis with direction cosines lambda, mu, nu relative to x, y, z, let I denote the moment of inertia about that axis. Let i, j, k denote the unit vectors along the x, y, z axes, respectively. Let r denote the radius vector from the origin to a chosen corner of the cube; in the solution we take the corner with positive x, y, z coordinates.
reference_solution:
By symmetry about the coordinate planes through the center of mass, the principal moments and products of inertia are

$$
I_{xx}=I_{0}
$$

$$
I_{yy}=I_{0}
$$

$$
I_{zz}=I_{0}
$$

$$
I_{xy}=0
$$

$$
I_{yz}=0
$$

$$
I_{zx}=0
$$

For an axis with direction cosines lambda, mu, nu, the moment of inertia is

$$
I=lambda^2 I_{xx}+mu^2 I_{yy}+nu^2 I_{zz}-2 mu nu I_{yz}-2 nu lambda I_{zx}-2 lambda mu I_{xy}
$$

Substituting the symmetry results gives

$$
I=(lambda^2+mu^2+nu^2) I_{0}
$$

Choose the corner in the first octant. The radius vector from the origin to that corner is

$$
r=a i+a j+a k
$$

Its magnitude is

$$
|r|=\sqrt{3} a
$$

Therefore the direction cosines of the body diagonal are

$$
\lambda=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}
$$

$$
\mu=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}
$$

$$
\nu=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}
$$

Thus

$$
I=I_{0}
$$

By definition of I_{corner}, we obtain

$$
I_{corner}=I_{0}
$$
model_response:
Let $M$ be the mass of the uniform cube.

### 1. Central moments of inertia

For a cube of side length $2a$, the moment about the $x$-axis is

$$
I_{xx}=\frac{1}{12}M\left((2a)^2+(2a)^2\right)
$$

$$
I_{xx}=\frac{2}{3}Ma^2
$$

By cubic symmetry,

$$
I_{yy}=\frac{2}{3}Ma^2
$$

$$
I_{zz}=\frac{2}{3}Ma^2
$$

Thus,

$$
I_0=\frac{2}{3}Ma^2
$$

Reflection symmetry about each coordinate plane gives

$$
I_{xy}=0
$$

$$
I_{yz}=0
$$

$$
I_{zx}=0
$$

### 2. Axis through the positive corner

The radius vector to the corner is

$$
r=a(i+j+k)
$$

Its magnitude is

$$
|r|=a\sqrt{3}
$$

Hence the direction cosines are

$$
\lambda=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}
$$

$$
\mu=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}
$$

$$
\nu=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}
$$

The moment of inertia about an axis with direction cosines $\lambda,\mu,\nu$ is

$$
I=I_{xx}\lambda^2+I_{yy}\mu^2+I_{zz}\nu^2-2I_{xy}\lambda\mu-2I_{yz}\mu\nu-2I_{zx}\nu\lambda
$$

For the body diagonal,

$$
I_{corner}=\frac{1}{3}\left(I_{xx}+I_{yy}+I_{zz}\right)
$$

Therefore,

$$
I_{corner}=\frac{2}{3}Ma^2
$$

### Final answer

$$
\boxed{I_{corner}=I_0}
$$

$$
\boxed{I_{corner}=I_0=\frac{2}{3}Ma^2}
$$

problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) A space station is made from a large cylinder of radius R_0 and length L, filled with air. The cylinder spins about its symmetry axis with angular speed ω so that the inward (centripetal) acceleration at the rim equals the gravitational acceleration at Earth's surface g. The absolute temperature T of the air is uniform throughout the cylinder. The air behaves as an ideal gas. Let p(r) be the air pressure and ρ(r) the mass density at radial distance r from the axis. Let M be the molar mass of air, R the universal gas constant, V the gas volume, and m the gas mass. Determine the ratio p(0)/p(R_0).
reference_solution:
Consider a thin cylindrical shell of air of radius r, thickness Δr, and length L. The pressure difference across its curved surfaces provides the centripetal force for the rotating air

$$[p(r+\Delta r) - p(r)] 2\pi r L = \omega^2 r 2\pi r L \rho \Delta r$$

Taking the limit as Δr tends to 0 gives

$$\frac{dp}{dr} = \rho \omega^2 r$$

The ideal gas equation of state is

$$p V = \frac{m}{M} R T$$

This implies

$$\rho = \frac{M}{R T} p$$

Therefore

$$\frac{dp}{dr} = \frac{M \omega^2}{R T} p r$$

Integrating from r = 0 to r = R_0 and from p(0) to p(R_0) yields

$$\int_{p(0)}^{p(R_0)} \frac{dp}{p} = \frac{M \omega^2}{R T} \int_0^{R_0} r dr$$

Hence

$$\ln\frac{p(R_0)}{p(0)} = \frac{M \omega^2 R_0^2}{2 R T}$$

At the rim, the centripetal acceleration equals g

$$\omega^2 R_0 = g$$

Substituting gives

$$\ln\frac{p(R_0)}{p(0)} = \frac{M R_0 g}{2 R T}$$

Therefore, the required ratio is

$$\frac{p(0)}{p(R_0)} = \exp\left(-\frac{M R_0 g}{2 R T}\right)$$
model_response:
### Solution

Radial force balance for the rotating air gives

$$
\frac{dp}{dr}=\rho(r)\omega^2r
$$

For an ideal gas at uniform temperature

$$
\rho(r)=\frac{Mp(r)}{RT}
$$

Substitution gives

$$
\frac{1}{p(r)}\frac{dp}{dr}=\frac{M\omega^2r}{RT}
$$

Integrating from the axis to the rim

$$
\ln\frac{p(R_0)}{p(0)}=\frac{M\omega^2R_0^2}{2RT}
$$

The rim acceleration equals $g$

$$
\omega^2R_0=g
$$

Therefore

$$
\ln\frac{p(R_0)}{p(0)}=\frac{MgR_0}{2RT}
$$

### Final Answer

$$
\boxed{\frac{p(0)}{p(R_0)}=\exp\left(-\frac{MgR_0}{2RT}\right)}
$$

AI_audit.reason: The model response exactly matches the valid reference result. Radial equilibrium and the isothermal ideal-gas relation give d(ln p)/dr=Mω²r/(RT), so ln[p(R₀)/p(0)]=Mω²R₀²/(2RT)=MgR₀/(2RT), hence p(0)/p(R₀)=exp[-MgR₀/(2RT)].

problem_statement:
A particle of mass m is constrained to move in a plane and is attracted to a fixed point P in this plane by a central force. The force is always directed toward P and has magnitude k/r^2, where r is the distance from P and k is a positive constant. Use plane polar coordinates (r, theta) with origin at P, where r is the radial coordinate and theta is the polar angle. Time is denoted by t, and overdots denote derivatives with respect to t. The generalized coordinates are q_i in {r, theta}, where the index i labels the coordinates. The kinetic energy is denoted by T, the potential energy by V with V(infinity)=0, and the Lagrangian by L=T-V. The conserved angular momentum about P is denoted by ell. The symbol s denotes a dummy radial integration variable when needed.

a) Using polar coordinates,write the Lagrangian of this particle.

b) Write Lagrangian equations for this particle and find at least one first integral.
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 Choose polar coordinates with origin at P in the plane of motion. The force is attractive with magnitude k/r^2 and V(infinity)=0, so the potential energy is
$$V(r)=-\int_\infty^r \left(-\frac{k}{s^2}\right) ds$$
which gives
$$V(r)=-\frac{k}{r}$$
The kinetic energy of the particle is
$$T=\frac{1}{2} m (\dot r^2+r^2 \dot \theta^2)$$
The Lagrangian is
$$L=T-V$$
so
$$L=\frac{1}{2} m (\dot r^2+r^2 \dot \theta^2)+\frac{k}{r}$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 Lagrange's equations for generalized coordinates q_i in {r, theta} are
$$\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot q_i}\right)-\frac{\partial L}{\partial q_i}=0$$
The equations of motion are
$$m \ddot r+\frac{k}{r^2}=0$$
$$\frac{d}{dt}(m r^2 \dot \theta)=0$$
A first integral obtained from the second equation is
$$m r^2 \dot \theta=\ell$$
which means that the angular momentum with respect to P is conserved
model_response:
### Step 1: Potential energy

The radial force is

$$
F_r=-\frac{k}{r^2}
$$

Using $F_r=-\frac{dV}{dr}$

$$
\frac{dV}{dr}=\frac{k}{r^2}
$$

With $V(\infty)=0$

$$
V(r)=-\int_r^\infty\frac{k}{s^2}ds
$$

$$
V(r)=-\frac{k}{r}
$$

### Step 2: Lagrangian

The kinetic energy in polar coordinates is

$$
T=\frac{1}{2}m\dot r^2+\frac{1}{2}mr^2\dot\theta^2
$$

Therefore

$$
L=\frac{1}{2}m\dot r^2+\frac{1}{2}mr^2\dot\theta^2+\frac{k}{r}
$$

### Step 3: Lagrange equations

For each generalized coordinate $q_i$

$$
\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q_i}-\frac{\partial L}{\partial q_i}=0
$$

For $r$

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot r}=m\dot r
$$

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial r}=mr\dot\theta^2-\frac{k}{r^2}
$$

Hence the radial equation is

$$
m\ddot r-mr\dot\theta^2+\frac{k}{r^2}=0
$$

For $\theta$

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial\theta}=0
$$

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot\theta}=mr^2\dot\theta
$$

Hence the angular equation is

$$
\frac{d}{dt}(mr^2\dot\theta)=0
$$

### First integral

Since $\theta$ is cyclic, angular momentum is conserved

$$
mr^2\dot\theta=\ell
$$

Equivalently

$$
\dot\theta=\frac{\ell}{mr^2}
$$

### Final answer

**a)**

$$
L=\frac{1}{2}m\dot r^2+\frac{1}{2}mr^2\dot\theta^2+\frac{k}{r}
$$

**b)**

$$
m\ddot r-mr\dot\theta^2+\frac{k}{r^2}=0
$$

$$
\frac{d}{dt}(mr^2\dot\theta)=0
$$

A first integral is

$$
mr^2\dot\theta=\ell
$$

problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) A particle of mass m and charge e moves in an isotropic three-dimensional harmonic oscillator potential with natural angular frequency ω_0. The trapping potential is V_trap = (1/2) m ω_0^2 r^2. The particle is simultaneously subjected to uniform magnetic and electric fields of magnitudes B and E that are mutually perpendicular. Choose Cartesian axes so that the magnetic field is along the z-axis and the electric field is along the x-axis. Use SI units throughout. Find the normal-mode angular vibration frequencies. Define ω_z as the z-direction frequency and ω_+, ω_- as the two in-plane normal-mode angular frequencies. Discuss the weak-field limit eB/m ≪ ω_0 and the strong-field limit eB/m ≫ ω_0.
reference_solution:
The fields may be generated by potentials A and Φ satisfying
$$
\nabla \times A = B k
$$
$$
- \nabla \Phi = E i
$$
A convenient gauge is
$$
A = \left( - \frac{1}{2} B y , \frac{1}{2} B x , 0 \right)
$$
$$
\Phi = - E x
$$
For an isotropic harmonic oscillator of natural angular frequency ω_0, the generalized potential is
$$
V = \frac{1}{2} m \omega_0^2 r^2 + e \Phi - e \dot r \cdot A
$$
with r = (x,y,z). The Lagrangian is
$$
L = T - V
$$
$$
L = \frac{1}{2} m ( \dot x^2 + \dot y^2 + \dot z^2 ) - \frac{1}{2} m \omega_0^2 ( x^2 + y^2 + z^2 ) + e E x + \frac{1}{2} e B ( - \dot x y + x \dot y )
$$
Lagrange's equations are
$$
\frac{d}{dt} \left( \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot q_i} \right) - \frac{\partial L}{\partial q_i} = 0
$$
The equations of motion are
$$
\ddot x + \omega_0^2 x - \frac{eB}{m} \dot y - \frac{eE}{m} = 0
$$
$$
\ddot y + \omega_0^2 y + \frac{eB}{m} \dot x = 0
$$

Solution for subproblem(a):
 A point (x_0,y_0) is in stable equilibrium if the first derivatives vanish and the quadratic form of second derivatives is positive definite. The conditions are

\frac{\partial V}{\partial x} = 0
$$
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
$$
y' = y

problem_statement:
A particle of mass m moves under uniform gravity on a smooth surface given by z = x^2 + y^2 - x y, where x, y, z are Cartesian coordinates and the z-axis is vertical, pointing upwards. The gravitational acceleration has magnitude g with SI units \unit{m/s^2}, and the gravitational potential energy is V = m g z. Time is denoted by t. In parts (b) and (c), small oscillations about the stable equilibrium are considered; the angular frequency is denoted by \omega, and the complex amplitudes in the trial solutions are x_0 and y_0. The normal-mode angular frequencies are denoted by \omega_1 and \omega_2.

a) Find the equations of motion of the particle.

b) Find the frequencies of the normal-modes for small oscillations about the position of stable equilibrium.

c) If the particle is displaced from equilibrium slightly and then released,what must be the ratio of the x and y displacements to guarantee that only the higher frequency normal-mode is excited?
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 The surface constraint is given by
$$z = x^2 + y^2 - x y$$
Differentiating with respect to time gives
$$\dot z = 2 x \dot x + 2 y \dot y - y \dot x - x \dot y$$
This can be written as
$$\dot z = \dot x (2 x - y) + \dot y (2 y - x)$$
The kinetic energy is
$$T = \frac{1}{2} m (\dot x^2 + \dot y^2 + \dot z^2)$$
Using the constraint, we have
$$\dot z^2 = \dot x^2 (2 x - y)^2 + \dot y^2 (2 y - x)^2 + 2 \dot x \dot y (2 x - y)(2 y - x)$$
Thus
$$T = \frac{1}{2} m [ \dot x^2 + \dot y^2 + \dot x^2 (2 x - y)^2 + \dot y^2 (2 y - x)^2 + 2 \dot x \dot y (2 x - y)(2 y - x) ]$$
The potential energy is
$$V = m g (x^2 + y^2 - x y)$$
The Lagrangian is
$$L = T - V$$
Lagrange's equations are
$$\frac{d}{dt} \bigg( \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot q_i} \bigg) - \frac{\partial L}{\partial q_i} = 0$$
Using q_1 = x and q_2 = y, the equations of motion are
$$\frac{d}{dt} [ \dot x + \dot x (2 x - y)^2 + \dot y (2 x - y)(2 y - x) ] = 2 \dot x^2 (2 x - y) - \dot y^2 (2 y - x) + 2 \dot x \dot y (2 y - x) - \dot x \dot y (2 x - y) - 2 g x + g y$$
$$\frac{d}{dt} [ \dot y + \dot y (2 y - x)^2 + \dot x (2 x - y)(2 y - x) ] = 2 \dot y^2 (2 y - x) - \dot x^2 (2 x - y) + 2 \dot x \dot y (2 x - y) - \dot x \dot y (2 y - x) - 2 g y + g x$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 From the potential energy we have
$$\frac{\partial V}{\partial x} = m g (2 x - y)$$
$$\frac{\partial V}{\partial y} = m g (2 y - x)$$
Equilibrium occurs at the origin x = 0, y = 0. For small oscillations about the origin, the linearized equations of motion are
$$\ddot x + 2 g x - g y = 0$$
$$\ddot y + 2 g y - g x = 0$$
Consider solutions of the form
$$x = x_0 e^{i \omega t}$$
$$y = y_0 e^{i \omega t}$$
The secular equation is
$$( g - \omega^2 )( 3 g - \omega^2 ) = 0$$
The normal-mode angular frequencies are
$$\omega_1 = \sqrt{g}$$
$$\omega_2 = \sqrt{3 g}$$

Solution for subproblem(c):
 From the eigenvector condition we have
$$\frac{y_0}{x_0} = \frac{2 g - \omega^2}{g}$$
For the higher frequency mode with \omega^2 = 3 g, the ratio is
$$\frac{y_0}{x_0} = -1$$
Therefore, the initial displacements of x and y must be equal in magnitude and opposite in sign so that only the higher frequency normal-mode is excited.

problem_statement:
A monochromatic transverse wave is emitted by a source at rest in the inertial frame κ. The wave has proper frequency ν and propagates at an angle θ=60^{\circ} with respect to the x-axis in κ. The speed of wave propagation is c. An observer is at rest in frame K', whose x'-axis is parallel to the x-axis of κ. The frame K' moves with speed v=\frac{4}{5}c along the +x direction relative to κ. Define β=\frac{v}{c} and γ=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-β^{2}}}. The observer measures the wave's frequency ν' and its angle of propagation θ' in K'. (a) Determine the measured frequency ν' in terms of the proper frequency ν. (b) Determine the angle of observation θ' in K'.

b) What is the angle of observation in the $K ^ { \prime }$ frame?
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(b):
 We use the Lorentz transformation of the wave four-vector from κ to K'. The frequency transforms as
$$β=\frac{v}{c}$$
$$γ=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-β^{2}}}$$
$$θ=60^{\circ}$$
$$\cos θ=\frac{1}{2}$$
$$ν'=γ ν \bigl(1-β \cos θ\bigr)$$
With v=\frac{4}{5}c we have
$$β=\frac{4}{5}$$
$$γ=\frac{5}{3}$$
Therefore
$$ν'=ν$$
The aberration of light gives the observed angle in K':
$$\cos θ'=\frac{\cos θ-β}{1-β \cos θ}$$
Substituting the values yields
$$\cos θ'=-\frac{1}{2}$$
Hence
$$θ'=120^{\circ}$$

problem_statement:

a) Consider monochromatic radiation emitted at the Sun with frequency \nu_s in \unit{Hz} and received at the Earth with frequency \nu_e in \unit{Hz}. Work in a static, weak gravitational field described by the metric components

$$
g_{00}=1+\frac{2\Phi}{c^2}
$$

$$
g_{11}=-1
$$

$$
g_{22}=-1
$$

$$
g_{33}=-1
$$

$$
g_{\mu\neq\nu}=0
$$

Here c is the speed of light in \unit{m/s}, and \Phi(r) is the gravitational potential energy per unit mass at position r. Let r_s denote a point on the Sun where the light is emitted and r_e denote a point on the Earth where the light is received. Let P_1 be the emission point and P_2 be the reception point, both at rest in the static field. Let t_0 be the coordinate time of emission of the first crest at P_1, t be the coordinate period between successive emitted crests, and T be the coordinate propagation time from P_1 to P_2. Let \tau be the proper period at P_1 measured by a standard clock co-moving with P_1, and let \tau' be the proper period at P_2 measured by a standard clock co-moving with P_2. Let \nu be the emitted frequency measured locally at P_1 and \nu' be the received frequency measured locally at P_2. Assume the field is static so that T is constant. Using this metric, derive the gravitational redshift, expressed as the fractional frequency shift (\nu_e-\nu_s)/\nu_s, as a function of the difference of gravitational potentials at the Sun and Earth.
reference_solution:
In a gravitational field it is possible to define a freely falling frame over a limited region that behaves as an inertial frame, and a standard clock at rest in such a frame measures the local proper time interval.

Consider an atom at rest at point P_1. If the emitted wave has coordinate period t, the local proper period at P_1 is

$$
\tau=t\sqrt{g_{00}(P_1)}
$$

The locally measured frequencies satisfy

$$

problem_statement:
Consider a very high energy scattering experiment involving two particles with the same rest mass m_0. In the laboratory frame, one particle is initially at rest and the other is incident with 3-momentum magnitude p and total energy E. Let c denote the speed of light. The center-of-mass (COM) frame is the frame in which the total 3-momentum is zero. Define beta^* = v^*/c as the speed parameter of the COM relative to the laboratory frame, where v^* is the COM speed. Let E^* denote the total energy of the two-particle system in the COM frame. Let \bar{E} denote the energy of each particle in the COM frame.

a) Find the velocity of the center of mass beta^* = v^*/c.

b) In the extreme relativistic limit p c \gg m_0 c^2, find the total energy E^* of the system in the center of mass frame (i.e. the frame in which the total 3-momentum is zero).
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 In the laboratory frame the system has total energy E + m_0 c^2 and total momentum p. The velocity of the center of mass, in units of c, is then
$$\beta^* = \frac{p c}{E + m_0 c^2}$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 The quantity (total energy)^2 minus (total momentum times c)^2 is invariant under Lorentz transformations. In the laboratory frame it is
$$(E + m_0 c^2)^2 - p^2 c^2$$
For the incident particle one has
$$E^2 - p^2 c^2 = m_0^2 c^4$$
Hence in the laboratory frame
$$(E + m_0 c^2)^2 - p^2 c^2 = 2 E m_0 c^2 + 2 m_0^2 c^4$$
In the center of mass frame the total momentum is zero, so the invariant equals
$$(2 \bar{E})^2$$
Equating the invariants gives
$$(2 \bar{E})^2 = 2 E m_0 c^2 + 2 m_0^2 c^4$$
The total COM energy is
$$E^* = 2 \bar{E}$$
Thus
$$E^* = \sqrt{2 E m_0 c^2 + 2 m_0^2 c^4}$$
In the extreme relativistic limit one has
$$E = \sqrt{p^2 c^2 + m_0^2 c^4}$$
and therefore
$$E \approx p c$$
Hence the COM energy approximations are
$$E^* \approx \sqrt{2 E m_0 c^2}$$
$$E^* \approx \sqrt{2 p m_0 c^3}$$
model_response:
### a) COM velocity

The laboratory-frame total energy and momentum are

$$
E_{\rm lab}=E+m_0c^2
$$

$$
p_{\rm lab}=p
$$

The COM speed satisfies

$$
v^*=\frac{p_{\rm lab}c^2}{E_{\rm lab}}
$$

Therefore

$$
v^*=\frac{pc^2}{E+m_0c^2}
$$

$$
\boxed{\beta^*=\frac{pc}{E+m_0c^2}}
$$

### b) COM energy

Energy-momentum invariance gives

$$
{E^*}^2=(E+m_0c^2)^2-p^2c^2
$$

For the incident particle,

$$
E^2=p^2c^2+m_0^2c^4
$$

Hence

$$
{E^*}^2=2m_0c^2(E+m_0c^2)
$$

In the extreme relativistic limit,

$$
E\approx pc
$$

$$
E+m_0c^2\approx pc
$$

Thus

$$
\boxed{E^*\approx\sqrt{2m_0c^2pc}}
$$

The energy of each particle in the COM frame is

$$
\boxed{\bar E\approx\sqrt{\frac{m_0c^2pc}{2}}}
$$

For $pc\gg m_0c^2$, $E\approx pc$ and $E+m_0c^2\approx pc$, so $E^*\approx\sqrt{2m_0pc^3}=\sqrt{2m_0c^2\cdot pc}$, exactly equivalent to the reference result. Its additional per-particle energy is also consistent: $\bar{E}=E^*/2\approx\sqrt{m_0c^2\cdot pc/2}$.

problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) A thin but very massive insulating disc has uniform surface charge density \(\sigma\) and radius \(R\). A point charge of magnitude \(+Q\) is located on the symmetry axis at axial distance \(z\) from the disc center. Using \(\varepsilon_0\) for the vacuum permittivity, derive an expression for the force \(F\) on the charge. Here, \(F\) denotes the axial component of the force on the charge, taken as positive along the +\(z\)-axis.
reference_solution:
Let the point charge +Q be at \((0,0,z)\) on the axis. The axial electric field produced by the disc at this point is

$$
E_z = \frac{\sigma}{2 \varepsilon_0} \left( 1 - \frac{z}{\sqrt{R^2 + z^2}} \right)
$$

The force on the point charge is

$$
F = Q E_z
$$

Thus

$$
F = \frac{\sigma Q}{2 \varepsilon_0} \left( 1 - \frac{z}{\sqrt{R^2 + z^2}} \right)
$$

By symmetry, the direction of this force is along the axis of the disc.
model_response:
### Solution

Treat the disc as concentric rings of radius $r$ and width $dr$:

$$
dq=2\pi r\sigma dr
$$

The axial electric-field contribution at the charge is

$$
dE_z=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{z\,dq}{(z^2+r^2)^{3/2}}
$$

Substituting $dq$ and integrating from $r=0$ to $r=R$:

$$
E_z=\frac{\sigma z}{2\varepsilon_0}\int_0^R\frac{r\,dr}{(z^2+r^2)^{3/2}}
$$

$$
\int_0^R\frac{r\,dr}{(z^2+r^2)^{3/2}}=\frac{1}{z}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{z^2+R^2}}
$$

Thus, for the charge on the positive side of the disc, $z>0$:

$$
E_z=\frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\left(1-\frac{z}{\sqrt{z^2+R^2}}\right)
$$

Using $F=QE_z$, the axial force is

$$
\boxed{F=\frac{Q\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\left(1-\frac{z}{\sqrt{z^2+R^2}}\right)}
$$

problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) A sphere of radius R carries a total charge Q uniformly distributed throughout its volume. Using Gauss's law, find the electric field vector both outside and inside the sphere. Use rho for the volume charge density, epsilon_0 for the vacuum permittivity, vec{r} for the position vector from the center, r=|vec{r}| for the radial distance, and vec{E} for the electric field.
reference_solution:
The volume charge density is
$$
\rho=\frac{Q}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3}
$$
Choose as a Gaussian surface a sphere of radius r concentric with the charged sphere; by symmetry vec{E} is radial. Gauss's law gives
$$
\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{S}=\frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}\int \rho dV
$$
For r\geq R,
$$
\vec{E}=\frac{Q\vec{r}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^3}
$$
For r\leq R,
$$
\vec{E}=\frac{Q\vec{r}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R^3}
$$
model_response:
### Charge density

$$
\rho=\frac{3Q}{4\pi R^3}
$$

By spherical symmetry,

$$
\vec{E}=E(r)\frac{\vec{r}}{r}
$$

### Outside the sphere: $r\geq R$

The enclosed charge is

$$
Q_{\rm enc}=Q
$$

Gauss’s law gives

$$
E(r)4\pi r^2=\frac{Q}{\epsilon_0}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\vec{E}=\frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0r^3}\vec{r}
$$

### Inside the sphere: $0\leq r<R$

The enclosed charge is

$$
Q_{\rm enc}=\frac{4\pi\rho r^3}{3}
$$

Gauss’s law gives

$$
E(r)4\pi r^2=\frac{4\pi\rho r^3}{3\epsilon_0}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\vec{E}=\frac{\rho}{3\epsilon_0}\vec{r}
$$

Using the total charge,

$$
\vec{E}=\frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0R^3}\vec{r}
$$

### Final answer

For $r\geq R$,

$$
\boxed{\vec{E}=\frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0r^3}\vec{r}}
$$

For $0\leq r<R$,

$$
\boxed{\vec{E}=\frac{\rho}{3\epsilon_0}\vec{r}}
$$

At the center,

$$
\vec{E}=0
$$

AI_audit.reason: The model response is physically and algebraically equivalent to the valid reference: outside, $\vec E=Q\vec r/(4\pi\epsilon_0 r^3)$; inside, $\vec E=\rho\vec r/(3\epsilon_0)=Q\vec r/(4\pi\epsilon_0R^3)$, using $\rho=3Q/(4\pi R^3)$. Its separate boundary convention (inside stated for $r<R$, outside for $r\ge R$) is harmless because the two expressions agree at $r=R$, and $\vec E=0$ at the center is correct.

problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) A charge Q is placed on a capacitor of capacitance C_1. One terminal is connected to ground and the other terminal (the free plate) is insulated and not connected to anything. The separation between the plates is increased so that the capacitance becomes C_2. The capacitances satisfy
$$
C_2 < C_1
$$
Define V_1 as the electric potential of the insulated plate relative to ground before the separation, and V_2 as the electric potential of the insulated plate relative to ground after the separation. Use Q for the charge on the insulated plate, C for capacitance, and V for the potential of the insulated plate relative to ground, related by
$$
Q = C V
$$
What happens to the potential on the free plate when the plates are separated? Express V_2 in terms of V_1
reference_solution:
During the separation, the insulated plate remains isolated, so its charge stays constant. Before separation
$$
Q = C_1 V_1
$$
After separation
$$
Q = C_2 V_2
$$
Since Q is unchanged
$$
C_1 V_1 = C_2 V_2
$$
Therefore
$$
V_2 = \frac{C_1}{C_2} V_1
$$

The insulated plate cannot exchange charge, so $Q$ remains constant

$$
Q=C_1V_1
$$

$$
Q=C_2V_2
$$

Therefore

$$
C_1V_1=C_2V_2
$$

$$
V_2=\frac{C_1}{C_2}V_1
$$

Since $C_2<C_1$

$$
V_2>V_1
$$

### Final Answer

The potential of the free plate increases

$$
\boxed{V_2=\frac{C_1}{C_2}V_1}
$$

problem_statement:
A cylinder of radius R and infinite length is made of a permanently polarized dielectric. The polarization vector is everywhere proportional to the radial position vector in cylindrical coordinates (r, θ, z) with basis unit vectors e_r, e_θ, e_z. The polarization is P = a r e_r, where a > 0 is a constant. The cylinder rotates about the z axis with angular velocity vector ω = ω e_z. This is a nonrelativistic problem with ω R << c. The outward unit normal on the cylindrical surface is n = e_r. The electric and magnetic fields are denoted by E and B. The bound volume charge density is ρ and the bound surface charge density is σ. When the cylinder spins, the material velocity is v = ω r e_θ. The volume current density is j = ρ v and the surface current density is K = σ v. The vacuum permittivity and permeability are ε_0 and μ_0, and c^2 = 1/(ε_0 μ_0). Let dW_e/dz and dW_m/dz denote, respectively, the electric and magnetic energy stored per unit length, and dW/dz the total electromagnetic energy per unit length. Let λ_tot be the total bound charge per unit length. For the magnetic field, define B_in(r) such that B = B_in(r) e_z for r < R and B_out(r) such that B = B_out(r) e_z for r > R.

a) Find the electric field E at a radius r both inside and outside the cylinder.

b) Find the magnetic field B at a radius r both inside and outside the cylinder.

c) What is the total electromagnetic energy stored per unit length of the cylinder,

i) before the cyliner started spinning? (ii) while it is spinning? Where did the extra energy come from?
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 From P = a r e_r, the bound volume and surface charge densities are computed by ρ = - ∇ · P and σ = n · P at r = R.
$$P = a r e_r$$
$$\rho = - \nabla \cdot P$$
$$\rho = - 2 a$$
$$\sigma = n \cdot P$$
$$\sigma = a R$$
The total bound charge per unit length is
$$\lambda_{tot} = - 2 a \pi R^2 + 2 \pi R \cdot a R$$
$$\lambda_{tot} = 0$$
By Gauss' law and cylindrical symmetry, the electric field inside is radial and linear in r, and it vanishes outside. The inside and outside fields are
$$E_{in}(r) = - \frac{a r}{\varepsilon_0} e_r$$
$$E_{out}(r) = 0$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 When the cylinder rotates, the material velocity is v = ω r e_θ, so the bound current densities are
$$v = \omega r e_\theta$$
$$j = \rho v$$
$$j = - 2 a \omega r e_\theta$$

problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) A cylindrical soft iron rod of length L and diameter d is bent into a circular shape of radius R, leaving an air gap of width s between the nearly meeting ends. Assume s << d and d << R, and neglect fringing. A coil of N turns is wound tightly around the iron rod, and a current I flows through the coil. The relative permeability of the iron is μ_r, and μ_0 is the permeability of free space. Let B be the magnetic flux density in the gap and H be the magnetic field strength used in Ampere's circuital law. Find B in the gap.
reference_solution:
Since s << d << R, magnetic leakage across the gap can be neglected, so the magnetic flux density in the gap equals that in the iron core.

$$
\oint H \cdot dl = NI
$$

Along the iron path H = \frac{B}{\mu_0 \mu_r} over length approximately 2 \pi R - s, and across the air gap H = \frac{B}{\mu_0} over length s, so

$$
NI = \frac{B}{\mu_0 \mu_r} (2 \pi R - s) + \frac{B}{\mu_0} s
$$

Solving for B gives

$$
B = \frac{\mu_r \mu_0 N I}{2 \pi R + (\mu_r - 1) s}
$$

$$

$$

For the air gap,

$$
H_{\rm gap}=\frac{B}{\mu_0}
$$

Ampère’s circuital law gives

$$
NI=H_{\rm iron}L+H_{\rm gap}s
$$

Substitution gives

$$
NI=\frac{BL}{\mu_0\mu_r}+\frac{Bs}{\mu_0}
$$

Therefore,

$$
B=\frac{\mu_0NI}{s+\frac{L}{\mu_r}}
$$

Since $L\approx2\pi R-s$, an equivalent form is

$$
B=\frac{\mu_0NI}{s+\frac{2\pi R-s}{\mu_r}}
$$

### Final Answer

$$
\boxed{B=\frac{\mu_0NI}{s+\frac{L}{\mu_r}}}
$$

Substituting gives

The mutual inductance is

$$

A straight conducting wire of mass m slides on frictionless contacts, completing a circuit with total resistance R. A constant external force of magnitude F is applied to the wire.  An emf is induced by the motion through the magnetic field
$$
\varepsilon = B l v
$$
The current in the circuit is
$$
I = \frac{\varepsilon}{R}
$$
The magnetic force opposing the motion has magnitude
$$
F_B = I l B
$$
The equation of motion is
$$
 m \frac{dv}{dt} = F - \frac{B^2 l^2}{R} v
$$
The general solution is
$$
 v(t) = \frac{R F}{B^2 l^2} + C \exp\bigg(-\frac{B^2 l^2}{m R} t\bigg)
$$
Using the initial condition v(0)=0 gives
$$
 C = -\frac{R F}{B^2 l^2}
$$
Thus the velocity is
$$
 v(t) = \frac{F R}{B^2 l^2} \Big(1 - \exp\big(-\frac{B^2 l^2}{m R} t\big)\Big)
$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 The current is
$$
 I(t) = \frac{B l v(t)}{R}
$$
Substituting v(t) from part (a) gives
$$
 I(t) = \frac{F}{B l} \Big(1 - \exp\big(-\frac{B^2 l^2}{m R} t\big)\Big)
$$
The direction of the current is such that the magnetic force on the wire opposes its motion, in accordance with Lenz's law

problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) Show that the force between two magnetic dipoles varies as the inverse fourth power of the distance between their centers, for any relative orientation in space. Assume the dipoles are small compared with their separation and the medium is vacuum. Definitions: m_1 and m_2 are the magnetic dipole moment vectors, \vec{r} is the displacement vector from the center of dipole m_2 to the center of dipole m_1, r is the magnitude of \vec{r}, \mu_0 is the vacuum permeability, \varphi_m is the magnetic scalar potential due to m_2, \vec{B} is the magnetic flux density produced by m_2 at the location of m_1, and \vec{F}_m is the force on dipole m_1. The gradient operator \nabla acts with respect to the observation point at the location of m_1.
reference_solution:
The magnetic scalar potential of dipole m_2 at the location of m_1 is
$$
\varphi_m = \frac{1}{4\pi} \frac{m_2 \cdot \vec{r}}{r^3}
$$
The magnetic field is
$$
\vec{B} = -\mu_0 \nabla \varphi_m
$$
The force on dipole m_1 in the external field \vec{B} is
$$
\vec{F}_m = \nabla \left( m_1 \cdot \vec{B} \right)
$$
Substituting \vec{B} gives
$$
\vec{F}_m = \nabla \left[ m_1 \cdot \left( -\mu_0 \nabla \varphi_m \right) \right]
$$
Extracting constants yields
$$
\vec{F}_m = -\mu_0 \nabla \left[ m_1 \cdot \nabla \varphi_m \right]
$$
Substituting \varphi_m gives
$$
\vec{F}_m = -\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \nabla \left[ m_1 \cdot \nabla \left( \frac{m_2 \cdot \vec{r}}{r^3} \right) \right]
$$
Using the vector identity
$$
\nabla \left( \frac{m_2 \cdot \vec{r}}{r^3} \right) = \frac{m_2}{r^3} - \frac{3 \vec{r} \left( m_2 \cdot \vec{r} \right)}{r^5}
$$
leads to
$$
\vec{F}_m = -\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \nabla \left[ m_1 \cdot \left( \frac{m_2}{r^3} - \frac{3 \vec{r} \left( m_2 \cdot \vec{r} \right)}{r^5} \right) \right]
$$
which simplifies to
$$
\vec{F}_m = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \nabla \left[ \frac{3 \left( m_1 \cdot \vec{r} \right) \left( m_2 \cdot \vec{r} \right)}{r^5} - \frac{m_1 \cdot m_2}{r^3} \right]
$$
Each term inside the gradient scales as r^{-3}, so taking the gradient introduces one more factor of 1/r. Therefore
$$
\vec{F}_m \propto \frac{1}{r^4}
$$
which holds for any relative orientation of the two dipoles under the stated assumptions.

problem_statement:
A stationary, solid copper plate of area A is subjected to a spatially uniform magnetic field B(t) perpendicular to the plate. The magnitude B increases with time. The magnetic flux through the plate is denoted by \Phi, the induced electromotive force by \varepsilon, and the magnetic field produced by the eddy currents by B_{ind}. Use Lenz's law to determine whether each statement is correct. For grading, let S_a, S_b, S_c \in {0,1} indicate whether statements (a), (b), and (c) are correct (1) or incorrect (0).

a) help the field increase

b) slow down the increase

c) do nothing
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 By Lenz's law, eddy currents oppose the change in magnetic flux and therefore do not assist the increase of the external field.
$$S_a=0$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 For a perpendicular, increasing field through area A, the flux and induced emf satisfy
$$\Phi=B A$$
$$\varepsilon=-\frac{d\Phi}{dt}$$
Because B increases with time,
$$\frac{d\Phi}{dt}>0$$
The induced eddy currents therefore produce a field opposing the increase, which slows it down.
$$S_b=1$$

Solution for subproblem(c):
 Eddy currents are induced and act to oppose the change, so they do not do nothing.
$$S_c=0$$

$$

$$

$$

\varepsilon=-\frac{d\Phi}{dt}
$$

Thus, the eddy currents produce $B_{ind}$ opposing the increase in $B$

$$
B_{ind}\text{ slows the increase of }B
$$

Therefore, (a) is incorrect, (b) is correct, and (c) is incorrect

### Final Answer

$$
S_a=0
$$

$$
S_b=1
$$

$$
S_c=0
$$

A secondary winding wrapped around the center of the solenoid has N' = 100 turns. The solenoid winding is connected to a load resistance R = 10^3\unit{\Omega}. A constant current I = 1\unit{A} flows in the secondary winding and is suddenly stopped at time t = 0^+. Define: n = N/l as the number of turns per unit length of the solenoid, B as the magnetic field inside the solenoid, \phi as the magnetic flux through one turn of the solenoid, \psi as the total flux linkage of the solenoid winding, \psi' as the total flux linkage of the secondary winding, L as the self-inductance of the solenoid, M as the mutual inductance between the windings, i(t) as the induced current in the solenoid after the interruption, q as the total charge that flows through the resistance during the transient, and t as time. reference_solution:
The number of turns per unit length is
$$
n=\frac{N}{l}
$$
The magnetic field inside the solenoid is
$$
B=\mu_0 n i
$$
The magnetic flux through one turn is
$$
\phi=B S
$$
The total flux linkage of the solenoid is
$$
\psi=N \phi
$$
Substituting gives
$$
\psi=\frac{N^2 \mu_0 S}{l} i
$$
The self-inductance is
$$
L=\frac{\psi}{i}
$$
Thus
$$
L=\frac{N^2 \mu_0 S}{l}
$$
Numerically
$$
L\approx 2.513\times 10^{-4} \unit{H}
$$
The total flux linkage of the secondary is
$$
\psi'=N' \phi
$$
The mutual inductance is
$$
M=\frac{\psi'}{i}
$$
Thus
$$
M=\frac{N N' \mu_0 S}{l}
$$
Numerically
$$
M\approx 2.513\times 10^{-5} \unit{H}
$$
When the secondary current is suddenly stopped, the solenoid obeys
$$
-\frac{d\psi'}{dt}=R i+L \frac{di}{dt}
$$
Equivalently
$$
-d\psi'=R i dt+L di
$$
With
$$
dq=i dt
$$
this becomes
$$
-d\psi'=R dq+L di
$$
Integrating from t=0^+ to t=\infty and using i(0^+)=0 and i(\infty)=0 gives
$$
-\Delta \psi'=R q
$$
Hence
$$
q=-\frac{\Delta \psi'}{R}
$$
Since \psi' changes from M I to 0, it follows that
$$
q=\frac{M I}{R}
$$
Numerically
$$
q\approx 2.76\times 10^{-7} \unit{C}
$$

problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) You have n identical storage cells, each with open-circuit voltage V and internal resistance R_i. The cells are grouped into sets of k series-connected cells each, where k is a positive integer that divides n. The n/k sets are then connected in parallel across a load resistance R. Let V_eq denote the open-circuit voltage of the combined source seen by the load, R_eq the equivalent internal resistance of the combined source, and P_max the maximum power delivered to the load. Find the value of k that maximizes the power delivered to R, and find the corresponding maximum power.
reference_solution:
For one series set of k cells, the open-circuit voltage is kV and the internal resistance is kR_i. With n/k such sets in parallel, the combined source has
$$
V_{eq}=kV
$$
The equivalent internal resistance is
$$
R_{eq}=\frac{kR_i}{n/k}
$$
$$
R_{eq}=\frac{k^2R_i}{n}
$$
For maximum power transfer, the load must match the source resistance
$$
R=R_{eq}
$$
Solving for k gives
$$
k=\sqrt{\frac{nR}{R_i}}
$$
Under this matching condition, the maximum power delivered to the load is
$$
P_{max}=\frac{V_{eq}^2}{4R_{eq}}
$$
$$
P_{max}=\frac{k^2V^2}{4R_{eq}}
$$
$$
P_{max}=\frac{k^2V^2}{4\left(\frac{k^2R_i}{n}\right)}
$$
$$
P_{max}=\frac{nV^2}{4R_i}
$$
model_response:
### Solution

For each series set,

$$
V_{\rm eq}=kV
$$

The resistance of each set is $kR_i$. With $n/k$ sets in parallel,

$$
R_{\rm eq}=\frac{k^2R_i}{n}
$$

The power delivered to $R$ is

$$
P(k)=\frac{k^2V^2R}{(R+\frac{k^2R_i}{n})^2}
$$

Treating $k$ as continuous,

$$
\frac{dP}{dk}=\frac{2kV^2R(R-\frac{k^2R_i}{n})}{(R+\frac{k^2R_i}{n})^3}
$$

Thus maximum power occurs when

$$
\frac{k^2R_i}{n}=R
$$

Hence the ideal value is

$$
k=\sqrt{\frac{nR}{R_i}}
$$

Since $k$ must be a positive divisor of $n$, the exact allowable choice is

$$
k_*\in\underset{k\in\mathbb N:k\mid n}{\arg\min}\left|\ln\left(\frac{k}{\sqrt{nR/R_i}}\right)\right|
$$

The corresponding maximum power is

$$
P_{\max}=\frac{k_*^2V^2R}{(R+\frac{k_*^2R_i}{n})^2}
$$

If $\sqrt{nR/R_i}$ is an integer divisor of $n$, then

$$
\boxed{k_*=\sqrt{\frac{nR}{R_i}}}
$$

and

$$
\boxed{P_{\max}=\frac{nV^2}{4R_i}}
$$

Its $k=\sqrt{nR/R_i}$ and $P_{\mathrm{max}}=nV^2/(4R_i)$ apply only when that value is an allowed divisor. In general, maximizing $P(k)=k^2V^2R/(R+k^2R_i/n)^2$ over $k\mid n$ requires the admissible divisor closest to $\sqrt{nR/R_i}$ in $\lvert\ln(k/k_0)\rvert$, as the model states, with the corresponding substituted power.

problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) An optical spectral line emitted by hydrogen atoms in a flame at room temperature is observed in the visible range with line-center frequency denoted by 
u_0. Estimate the Doppler width \Delta 
u due to thermal motion and identify the closest option from the set {10^{6}, 10^{9}, 10^{13}, 10^{16}} \unit{Hz}. Definitions and data: k is Boltzmann's constant, T is the absolute temperature, m is the mass of a hydrogen atom, c is the speed of light, v_{rms} is the root-mean-square speed, and  eta=v_{rms}/c. Use the nonrelativistic Doppler estimate \Delta 
u \approx 
u_0  eta with 
u_0 \approx 10^{14} \unit{Hz}. Take k=8.6	imes 10^{-5} \unit{eV/K}, T=300 \unit{K}, and mc^{2}\approx 10^{9} \unit{eV}.
reference_solution:
By equipartition of energy for translational motion we have
$$
\frac{m v_{rms}^{2}}{2}=\frac{3 k T}{2}
$$
Define the dimensionless speed
$$
\beta=\frac{v_{rms}}{c}
$$
From equipartition this gives
$$
\frac{v_{rms}}{c}=\sqrt{\frac{3 k T}{m c^{2}}}
$$
Use the given constants
$$
k=8.6\times 10^{-5} \unit{eV/K}
$$
$$
T=300 \unit{K}
$$
$$
mc^{2}\approx 10^{9} \unit{eV}
$$
Hence
$$
\beta\approx 10^{-5}
$$
The Doppler width is estimated by
$$
\Delta \nu=\nu_{0} \beta
$$
For visible light take
$$
\nu_{0}\approx 10^{14} \unit{Hz}
$$
Therefore
$$
\Delta \nu\approx 10^{9} \unit{Hz}
$$
Thus, the closest option is 10^{9} \unit{Hz}.

$$\beta\approx8.8\times10^{-6}$$

The Doppler width is

$$\Delta\nu\approx\nu_0\beta$$

$$\Delta\nu\approx(10^{14}\unit{Hz})(8.8\times10^{-6})$$

$$\Delta\nu\approx8.8\times10^8\unit{Hz}$$
