The closest option is

$$\boxed{\Delta\nu\approx10^9\unit{Hz}}$$

problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) A spin-1/2 particle with magnetic moment mu = mu_0 s is placed in a uniform magnetic field B pointing along the x axis. Work in the (s^2, s_x) representation, i.e., the eigenbasis of s_x. Let s = (s_x, s_y, s_z) denote the spin operators, with s_k = (1/2) sigma_k where sigma_k are the Pauli matrices in this basis. Let the time-dependent spinor be psi(t) = (a(t), b(t))^T in this basis. At t = 0 the particle is found to have s_z = +1/2. Here mu_0 is a constant, hbar is the reduced Planck constant, and i is the imaginary unit. Find the probabilities at time t of measuring s_y = ±1/2.
reference_solution:
In the (s^2, s_x) representation the Pauli matrices are
$$
\sigma_x=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}
$$
$$
\sigma_y=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}
$$
$$
\sigma_z=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}
$$
The spin operators satisfy
$$
s_k=\frac{1}{2}\sigma_k
$$
Normalized eigenvectors with eigenvalue +\frac{1}{2} are
$$
\nu_{x+}=\binom{1}{0}$$
$$
\nu_{y+}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\binom{1}{1}
$$
$$
\nu_{z+}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\binom{1}{i}
$$
The Hamiltonian is
$$
H=-\pmb{\mu}\cdot B
$$
Since B points along x and \pmb{\mu}=\mu_0 s, we have
$$
H=-\mu_0 B s_x
$$
In matrix form
$$
H=-\frac{\mu_0 B}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}
$$
Let
$$
\psi(t)=\binom{a(t)}{b(t)}
$$
The Schr\"odinger equation is
$$
i\hbar\frac{d}{dt}\psi(t)=H\psi(t)
$$
The initial condition from s_z=+\frac{1}{2} is
$$
\psi(0)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\binom{1}{i}
$$
Solving the decoupled equations gives
$$
a(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\exp\left(i\frac{\mu_0 B t}{2\hbar}\right)
$$
$$
b(t)=\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}\exp\left(-i\frac{\mu_0 B t}{2\hbar}\right)
$$
Define
$$
\alpha=\frac{\mu_0 B t}{2\hbar}
$$
The amplitude for s_y=+\frac{1}{2} is
$$
c_{+}(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\end{pmatrix}\binom{a(t)}{b(t)}
$$
Using the expressions for a(t), b(t) we obtain
$$
c_{+}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\left(\exp(i\alpha)+i\exp(-i\alpha)\right)
$$
The probability is
$$
P_{+}(t)=|c_{+}(t)|^2
$$
Using
$$
\left|\exp(i\alpha)+i\exp(-i\alpha)\right|^2=2\left(1+\sin(2\alpha)\right)
$$
we find
$$
P_{+}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\left(1+\sin\frac{\mu_0 B t}{\hbar}\right)
$$
Similarly
$$
P_{-}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\sin\frac{\mu_0 B t}{\hbar}\right)
$$
model_response:
### Solution

In the $s_x$ eigenbasis,

$$
s_x=\frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}
$$

$$
s_y=\frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}0&i\\-i&0\end{pmatrix}
$$

$$
s_z=\frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}
$$

The Hamiltonian is

$$
H=-\boldsymbol{\mu}\cdot\boldsymbol{B}
$$

$$
H=-\mu_0Bs_x
$$

The initial state $s_z=+1/2$ is

$$
\psi(0)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}
$$

The component equations are

$$
i\hbar\frac{da}{dt}=-\frac{\mu_0B}{2}a
$$

$$
i\hbar\frac{db}{dt}=\frac{\mu_0B}{2}b
$$

Thus,

$$
a(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\exp{\left(\frac{i\mu_0Bt}{2\hbar}\right)}
$$

$$
b(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\exp{\left(-\frac{i\mu_0Bt}{2\hbar}\right)}
$$

The normalized $s_y$ eigenstates are

$$
\lvert s_y=+1/2\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}i\\1\end{pmatrix}
$$

$$
\lvert s_y=-1/2\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}-i\\1\end{pmatrix}
$$

Therefore,

$$
P_{+}(t)=\left|\langle s_y=+1/2\vert\psi(t)\rangle\right|^2
$$

$$
P_{+}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\left[1+\sin{\left(\frac{\mu_0Bt}{\hbar}\right)}\right]
$$

$$
P_{-}(t)=\left|\langle s_y=-1/2\vert\psi(t)\rangle\right|^2
$$

$$
P_{-}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\left[1-\sin{\left(\frac{\mu_0Bt}{\hbar}\right)}\right]
$$

### Final answer

$$
\boxed{P\left(s_y=+\frac{1}{2}\right)=\frac{1}{2}\left[1+\sin{\left(\frac{\mu_0Bt}{\hbar}\right)}\right]}
$$

$$
\boxed{P\left(s_y=-\frac{1}{2}\right)=\frac{1}{2}\left[1-\sin{\left(\frac{\mu_0Bt}{\hbar}\right)}\right]}
$$

problem_statement:
Using the Bohr model of the atom. Let m be the electron mass, e be the magnitude of the electron charge, epsilon_0 be the vacuum permittivity, and \hbar be the reduced Planck constant. For the He^+ ion the nuclear charge number is Z=2. Let n be the principal quantum number (a positive integer), r be the orbital radius, v be the orbital speed, and L_\phi be the orbital angular momentum. Let l be the orbital angular momentum quantum number. In part (b), let A be the orbit area, \omega be the angular velocity, T be the orbital period, I be the current due to the electron’s orbital motion, \mu be the magnetic moment, and B be the magnitude of a uniform external magnetic field. Let \phi denote the azimuthal angle used in the area integral. Define E_n as the energy of the nth Bohr level and \Delta E as the interaction energy (energy shift) in the magnetic field. Neglect the electron spin throughout.

a) derive an expression for the energy levels of the He^{+} ion.

b) calculate the energies of the l = 1 state in a magnetic field, neglecting the electron spin.
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 Bohr quantization of the orbital angular momentum gives
$$L_\phi=m v r$$
$$L_\phi=n \hbar$$
The centripetal force is provided by the Coulomb attraction for Z=2
$$m \frac{v^2}{r}=\frac{2 e^2}{4 \pi \epsilon_0 r^2}$$
The total energy is
$$E_n=\frac{1}{2} m v^2-\frac{2 e^2}{4 \pi \epsilon_0 r}$$
Using the relations above, this becomes
$$E_n=-\frac{1}{2} m v^2$$
and finally
$$E_n=-\frac{2 m e^4}{(4 \pi \epsilon_0)^2 n^2 \hbar^2}$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 The area of the electron orbit is
$$A=\int_0^{2 \pi} \frac{1}{2} r^2 d\phi$$
Using d\phi=\omega dt, this becomes
$$A=\frac{1}{2} \int_0^T r^2 \omega dt$$
With
$$L_\phi=m r^2 \omega$$
one finds
$$A=\frac{L_\phi}{2 m} T$$
For l=1,
$$L_\phi=\hbar$$
The magnetic moment due to the orbital motion is
$$\mu=I A$$
with
$$I=-\frac{e}{T}$$
which gives
$$\mu=-\frac{e \hbar}{2 m}$$
The interaction energies for the three allowed orientations relative to the field of magnitude B are
$$\Delta E=\frac{e \hbar}{2 m} B$$
$$\Delta E=0$$
$$\Delta E=-\frac{e \hbar}{2 m} B$$
model_response:
## a) Energy levels of the \(\mathrm{He}^{+}\) ion

Coulomb attraction provides the centripetal force:

$$
\frac{mv^2}{r}=\frac{Ze^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0r^2}
$$

Bohr quantization gives:

$$
mvr=n\hbar
$$

Thus,

$$
r=\frac{4\pi\epsilon_0n^2\hbar^2}{mZe^2}
$$

The kinetic energy is:

$$
K=\frac{1}{2}mv^2
$$

Using the force equation:

$$
K=\frac{Ze^2}{8\pi\epsilon_0r}
$$

The electrostatic potential energy is:

$$
U=-\frac{Ze^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0r}
$$

Therefore,

$$
E_n=K+U
$$

$$
E_n=-\frac{Ze^2}{8\pi\epsilon_0r}
$$

Substitution of the orbital radius gives:

$$
E_n=-\frac{mZ^2e^4}{2(4\pi\epsilon_0)^2\hbar^2n^2}
$$

For \(\mathrm{He}^{+}\), $Z=2$:

$$
E_n=-\frac{2me^4}{(4\pi\epsilon_0)^2\hbar^2n^2}
$$

## b) Energies of the \(l=1\) state in a magnetic field

The orbit area is:

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{2\pi}r^2d\phi
$$

$$
A=\pi r^2
$$

The orbital period is:

$$
T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}
$$

The electron produces the conventional current:

$$
I=-\frac{e}{T}
$$

$$
I=-\frac{e\omega}{2\pi}
$$

The orbital magnetic moment is:

$$
\mu=IA
$$

$$
\mu=-\frac{e\omega r^2}{2}
$$

Since the orbital angular momentum is $L_\phi=m\omega r^2$:

$$
\mu=-\frac{e}{2m}L_\phi
$$

Taking the magnetic field along the quantization axis, the interaction energy is:

$$
\Delta E=-\mu B
$$

Let $m_l$ be the magnetic quantum number, with $L_\phi=m_l\hbar$:

$$
\Delta E=m_l\frac{e\hbar B}{2m}
$$

For $l=1$:

$$
m_l=-1,0,1
$$

Hence the three energies are:

$$
E_{n,-1}=E_n-\frac{e\hbar B}{2m}
$$

$$
E_{n,0}=E_n
$$

$$
E_{n,1}=E_n+\frac{e\hbar B}{2m}
$$

## Final answer

$$
E_n=-\frac{2me^4}{(4\pi\epsilon_0)^2\hbar^2n^2}
$$

$$
E_{n,m_l}=-\frac{2me^4}{(4\pi\epsilon_0)^2\hbar^2n^2}+m_l\frac{e\hbar B}{2m}
$$

$$
m_l=-1,0,1
$$

AI_audit.reason: The model’s result is physically and algebraically correct. For an electron, $\boldsymbol{\mu}_L=-\frac{e}{2m}\mathbf{L}$, so with $B$ along the quantization axis, $\Delta E=-\boldsymbol{\mu}_L\cdot\mathbf{B}=\frac{m_l e\hbar B}{2m}$. Thus the $l=1$ levels have shifts $-\frac{e\hbar B}{2m},0,+\frac{e\hbar B}{2m}$, exactly equivalent to the reference, and its He+ energy $E_n=-\frac{2me^4}{(4\pi\epsilon_0)^2\hbar^2n^2}$ also matches.

problem_statement:
A furnace contains atomic sodium at low pressure and temperature T=2000\unit{K}. Consider only three energy levels of sodium, with energies measured relative to the ground state: 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s: ^2S at E_0=0\unit{eV} (ground state), 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3p: ^2P at E_1=2.10\unit{eV}, and 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 4s: ^2S at E_2=3.18\unit{eV}. Define E_0, E_1, E_2 as the level energies of the 3s, 3p, and 4s states, respectively. Let T be the temperature, k the Boltzmann constant, e the elementary charge, c the speed of light in vacuum, and \hbar the reduced Planck constant. For a radiative transition k→i, define the angular frequency \omega_{ki}=(E_k−E_i)/\hbar, the Einstein A coefficient for spontaneous emission A_{ik}, the Einstein B coefficient for absorption B_{ik}, the level population N_i, and the spectral line intensity I_{ik}. Let g_i denote the degeneracy of level i. Magnetic quantum numbers are denoted m_k and m_i. The electric-dipole operator is r. For fine-structure sublevels with total angular momentum J, the degeneracy factor is g_J=2J+1; for the ^2P term there are J=3/2 and J=1/2 sublevels. Assume Boltzmann equilibrium populations N_i proportional to g_i exp(−E_i/(kT)). For absorption, the incident radiation has spectral energy density \rho(\omega); in part (b) it is flat so \rho(\omega) is constant over the relevant frequencies.

a) What are the photon energies of the emission lines present in the spectrum? What are their relative intensities? (Give appropriate expressions and evaluate them approximately as time permits).

b) Continuous radiation with a flat spectrum is now passed through the furnace and the absorption spectrum observed. What spectral lines are observed? Find their relative intensities.(UC, Berkeley)
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 There are two electric-dipole emission transitions: 3p→3s and 4s→3p. Their photon energies are
$$E_{10}=E_1-E_0$$
$$E_{10}=2.10\unit{eV}$$
$$E_{21}=E_2-E_1$$
$$E_{21}=1.08\unit{eV}$$
The spontaneous-emission probability for k\to i is
$$A_{ik}=\frac{e^2\omega_{ki}^3}{3\hbar^2 c^3}\frac{1}{g_k}\sum_{m_k,m_i}|\langle i m_i| r | k m_k\rangle|^2$$
with
$$\omega_{ki}=\frac{E_k-E_i}{\hbar}$$
The emission line intensity scales as
$$I_{ik}\propto N_k\hbar\omega_{ki}A_{ik}$$
with level populations
$$N_i\propto g_i\exp\left(-\frac{E_i}{kT}\right)$$
For the ^2P term there are J=\frac{3}{2} and J=\frac{1}{2} sublevels. Suppose the dipole matrix elements and sublevel statistical weights for the two emission lines are approximately equal. Then the intensity ratio is
$$\frac{I_{01}}{I_{12}}=\left(\frac{\omega_{10}}{\omega_{21}}\right)^4\exp\left(\frac{E_{21}}{kT}\right)$$
Numerically,
$$\frac{I_{01}}{I_{12}}\approx\left(\frac{2.10}{1.08}\right)^4\exp\left(\frac{1.08\unit{eV}}{8.6\times10^{-5}\unit{eV/K}\times2000\unit{K}}\right)$$
$$\frac{I_{01}}{I_{12}}\approx8\times10^3$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 With a flat incident spectrum, \rho(\omega) is constant. The absorption lines observed are 3s→3p and 3p→4s. The absorption-line intensity is
$$I_{ik}\propto B_{ik}N_k\rho(\omega_{ik})\hbar\omega_{ik}$$
where
$$B_{ik}=\frac{4\pi^2 e^2}{3\hbar^2}\frac{1}{g_k}\sum_{m_k,m_i}|\langle i m_i| r | k m_k\rangle|^2$$
The intensity ratio is
$$\frac{I_{10}}{I_{21}}=\frac{B_{10}N_0\omega_{10}}{B_{21}N_1\omega_{21}}$$
Assuming comparable matrix elements and statistical weights,
$$\frac{I_{10}}{I_{21}}\approx\left(\frac{\omega_{10}}{\omega_{21}}\right)\exp\left(\frac{E_{10}}{kT}\right)$$
Numerically,
$$\frac{I_{10}}{I_{21}}\approx\left(\frac{2.10}{1.08}\right)\exp\left(\frac{2.10\unit{eV}}{8.62\times10^{-5}\unit{eV/K}\times2000\unit{K}}\right)$$
$$\frac{I_{10}}{I_{21}}\approx4\times10^5$$
model_response:
### 1. Allowed electric-dipole transitions

The electric-dipole selection rule is

$$
\Delta l=\pm1
$$

Thus, the allowed transitions are \(3p\leftrightarrow3s\) and \(4s\leftrightarrow3p\). The direct \(4s\leftrightarrow3s\) transition is forbidden.

The photon energies are

$$
\varepsilon_{10}=E_1-E_0
$$

$$
\varepsilon_{10}=2.10\unit{eV}
$$

$$
\varepsilon_{21}=E_2-E_1
$$

$$
\varepsilon_{21}=1.08\unit{eV}
$$

No electric-dipole line occurs at \(3.18\unit{eV}\).

### 2. Equilibrium populations

The term degeneracies are

$$
g_0=2
$$

$$
g_1=2+4=6
$$

$$
g_2=2
$$

At \(T=2000\unit{K}\),

$$
kT\approx0.172\unit{eV}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{N_1}{N_0}=\frac{g_1}{g_0}\exp\left(-\frac{E_1-E_0}{kT}\right)
$$

$$
\frac{N_1}{N_0}\approx1.53\times10^{-5}
$$

$$
\frac{N_2}{N_1}=\frac{g_2}{g_1}\exp\left(-\frac{E_2-E_1}{kT}\right)
$$

$$
\frac{N_2}{N_1}\approx6.32\times10^{-4}
$$

$$
\frac{N_2}{N_0}\approx9.7\times10^{-9}
$$

Define the summed dipole strength by

$$
S_{ik}=\sum_{m_i,m_k}\left|\langle i,m_i|r|k,m_k\rangle\right|^2
$$

The Einstein coefficients satisfy

$$
A_{ik}=\frac{4e^2\omega_{ki}^3S_{ik}}{3\hbar c^3g_k}
$$

$$
B_{ik}=\frac{4\pi^2e^2S_{ik}}{3\hbar^2g_i}
$$

### 3. Emission spectrum

The emitted line intensity is

$$
I_{ik}^{e}\propto N_kA_{ik}\hbar\omega_{ki}
$$

Hence,

$$
\frac{I_{12}^{e}}{I_{01}^{e}}=\frac{N_2}{N_1}\frac{A_{12}}{A_{01}}\frac{E_2-E_1}{E_1-E_0}
$$

$$
\frac{I_{12}^{e}}{I_{01}^{e}}\approx3.25\times10^{-4}\frac{A_{12}}{A_{01}}
$$

Equivalently, in terms of dipole strengths,

$$
\frac{I_{12}^{e}}{I_{01}^{e}}=\exp\left(-\frac{E_2-E_1}{kT}\right)\left(\frac{\omega_{21}}{\omega_{10}}\right)^4\frac{S_{12}}{S_{01}}
$$

$$
\frac{I_{12}^{e}}{I_{01}^{e}}\approx1.33\times10^{-4}\frac{S_{12}}{S_{01}}
$$

Thus the \(2.10\unit{eV}\) line is overwhelmingly stronger than the \(1.08\unit{eV}\) line.

Each line group contains two fine-structure components. In \(LS\) coupling their approximate intensity ratio is

$$
I_{J=3/2}:I_{J=1/2}=2:1
$$

### 4. Absorption spectrum

Absorption occurs at the same two photon energies:

$$
3s\rightarrow3p:\quad2.10\unit{eV}
$$

$$
3p\rightarrow4s:\quad1.08\unit{eV}
$$

For flat \(\rho(\omega)\),

$$
I_{ik}^{a}\propto N_iB_{ik}\rho(\omega_{ki})\hbar\omega_{ki}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{I_{12}^{a}}{I_{01}^{a}}=\frac{N_1}{N_0}\frac{B_{12}}{B_{01}}\frac{E_2-E_1}{E_1-E_0}
$$

$$
\frac{I_{12}^{a}}{I_{01}^{a}}\approx7.86\times10^{-6}\frac{B_{12}}{B_{01}}
$$

Equivalently,

$$
\frac{I_{12}^{a}}{I_{01}^{a}}=\exp\left(-\frac{E_1-E_0}{kT}\right)\frac{\omega_{21}}{\omega_{10}}\frac{S_{12}}{S_{01}}
$$

$$
\frac{I_{12}^{a}}{I_{01}^{a}}\approx2.62\times10^{-6}\frac{S_{12}}{S_{01}}
$$

### Final answer

The emission and absorption spectra contain lines at

$$
2.10\unit{eV}
$$

$$
1.08\unit{eV}
$$

The \(3.18\unit{eV}\) \(3s\leftrightarrow4s\) line is electric-dipole forbidden. The \(1.08\unit{eV}\) line is strongly suppressed because the \(3p\) and \(4s\) populations are very small. A fully numerical ratio between the two line groups requires the radial dipole-strength ratio \(S_{12}/S_{01}\).

AI_audit.reason: The model’s general intensity ratios are correct: $I(4s\to3p)/I(3p\to3s)=e^{-(E2-E1)/kT}(\omega_{21}/\omega_{10})^4(S_{12}/S_{01})\approx1.33\times10^{-4}(S_{12}/S_{01})$, and $I(3p\to4s)/I(3s\to3p)=e^{-(E1-E0)/kT}(\omega_{21}/\omega_{10})(S_{12}/S_{01})\approx2.62\times10^{-6}(S_{12}/S_{01})$. Setting the dipole strengths equal, as the reference conditionally assumes, gives the inverse ratios $\approx7.5\times10^3$ and $\approx3.8\times10^5$, matching its $8\times10^3$ and $4\times10^5$ estimates. Retaining the unspecified strength ratio is more general and should have been accepted.

problem_statement:
For Zn, let E_K, E_{L_I}, E_{L_{II}}, and E_{L_{III}} denote the threshold (binding) energies of the K and L absorption edges. The given values are:
$$E_K=9.67\unit{keV}$$
$$E_{L_I}=1.21\unit{keV}$$
$$E_{L_{II}}=1.05\unit{keV}$$
$$E_{L_{III}}=1.03\unit{keV}$$
Determine the wavelength \lambda_{K\alpha} of the K_{\alpha} line. The K level corresponds to n=1, the three L levels correspond to the different states with n=2, and the K_{\alpha} line corresponds to a transition from the lowest L level L_{III} to the K level. If Zn is bombarded by monoenergetic electrons with kinetic energy E_e, determine the following for E_e=5\unit{keV}:
- the wavelength \lambda_{min} of the shortest X-ray line (bremsstrahlung cutoff), and
- the wavelength \lambda_{char,min} of the shortest characteristic X-ray line which can be emitted.
Use h for Planck's constant and c for the speed of light. Let E_{max} denote the maximum bremsstrahlung photon energy and E_{char,max} denote the maximum characteristic photon energy. In this problem, E_{max}=E_e.

a) the wavelength of the shortest X-ray line, and

b) the wavelength of the shortest characteristic X-ray line which can be emitted. Note: The K level corresponds to n = 1, the three L- levels to the different states with n = 2. The absorption edges are the lowest energies for which X- rays can be absorbed by ejection of an electron from the corresponding level. The K_{\alpha} line corresponds to a transition from the lowest L level.
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 The minimum X-ray wavelength that can be emitted by bombarding the atoms with 5-keV electrons is
$$E_{max}=5\unit{keV}$$
$$\lambda_{min}=\frac{hc}{E_{max}}$$
$$hc=12.41\unit{keV\cdot\AA}$$
$$\lambda_{min}=2.482\unit{\AA}$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 It is possible to excite electrons on energy levels other than the K level by bombardment with 5-keV electrons and cause the emission of characteristic X-rays when the atoms de-excite. The highest-energy characteristic X-rays have photon energy equal to the L_I edge:
$$E_{char,max}=E_{L_I}$$
$$E_{L_I}=1.21\unit{keV}$$
The corresponding shortest characteristic wavelength is
$$\lambda_{char,min}=\frac{hc}{E_{char,max}}$$
$$hc=12.41\unit{keV\cdot\AA}$$
$$\lambda_{char,min}=10.26\unit{\AA}$$
model_response:
### \(K_{\alpha}\) wavelength

The photon energy is the difference between the K and \(L_{III}\) binding energies

Using $hc=1.23984\unit{keV\,nm}$

$$\lambda_{K\alpha}=0.1435\unit{nm}$$

The maximum bremsstrahlung photon energy equals the electron kinetic energy

$$E_{max}=E_e$$

$$E_{max}=5.00\unit{keV}$$

$$\lambda_{min}=\frac{hc}{E_{max}}$$

$$\lambda_{min}=0.2480\unit{nm}$$

### b) Shortest characteristic X-ray wavelength

Since $E_e<E_K$, no K-shell vacancy can be produced. Since $E_e>E_{L_I}$, the deepest accessible level is \(L_I\)

$$E_{char,max}=E_{L_I}$$

$$E_{char,max}=1.21\unit{keV}$$

The L_I edge is only the series-limit/ionization energy, not a discrete emitted line; outer-shell binding energies and allowed transitions are needed to determine the shortest characteristic line. problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) Approximate the molecule 1H35Cl as a rigid dumbbell with internuclear separation r = 1.29×10^{-10} \unit{m}. Use m_H = 1 amu and m_Cl = 35 amu with 1 amu = 1.67×10^{-27} \unit{kg}, and Planck's constant h = 6.6×10^{-34} \unit{J s}. Let I be the moment of inertia, \mu the reduced mass, c the speed of light, J the rotational quantum number, \nu the frequency of the J → J − 1 transition, and \Delta \nu the frequency separation between adjacent rotational lines to be reported as the final answer. Let \hbar denote the reduced Planck constant, defined as h divided by 2\pi. The rotational constant B is defined by B = \hbar^2/(2 I h c).
reference_solution:
The moment of inertia of the molecule is
$$
I = \mu r^2
$$
The reduced mass is
$$
\mu = \frac{m_{Cl} m_H}{m_{Cl} + m_H}
$$
The chlorine mass is
$$
m_{Cl} = 35 \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27} \unit{kg}
$$
The hydrogen mass is
$$
m_H = 1 \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27} \unit{kg}
$$
The bond length is
$$
r = 1.29 \times 10^{-10} \unit{m}
$$
Hence
$$
I = \frac{35}{36} \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27} \times \left(1.29 \times 10^{-10}\right)^2 \unit{kg m^2}
$$
Numerically
$$
I = 2.7 \times 10^{-47} \unit{kg m^2}
$$
The line frequency for the J \to J - 1 transition is
$$
\nu = \frac{h c B J(J + 1) - h c B J(J - 1)}{h}
$$
Thus
$$
\nu = 2 c B J
$$
With
$$
B = \frac{\hbar^2}{2 I h c}
$$
It follows that
$$
\nu = \frac{\hbar^2}{I h} J
$$
Therefore the separation between adjacent rotational lines is
$$
\Delta \nu = 2 c B
$$
Equivalently
$$
\Delta \nu = \frac{\hbar^2}{h I}
$$
And
$$
\Delta \nu = \frac{h}{4 \pi^2 I}
$$
Substituting the values gives
$$
\Delta \nu = \frac{6.6 \times 10^{-34} \unit{J s}}{4 \pi^2 \times 2.7 \times 10^{-47} \unit{kg m^2}}
$$
Hence
$$
\Delta \nu = 6.2 \times 10^{11} \unit{Hz}
$$
model_response:
### Reduced mass

$$
\mu=\frac{m_Hm_{Cl}}{m_H+m_{Cl}}
$$

$$
\mu=\frac{35}{36}(1.67\times10^{-27})\unit{kg}
$$

$$
\mu=1.62\times10^{-27}\unit{kg}
$$

### Moment of inertia

$$
I=\mu r^2
$$

$$
I=(1.62\times10^{-27})(1.29\times10^{-10})^2\unit{kg\,m^2}
$$

$$
I=2.70\times10^{-47}\unit{kg\,m^2}
$$

### Rotational transition frequency

The rotational energy for quantum number $J$ is

$$
E_J=\frac{\hbar^2}{2I}J(J+1)
$$

For the transition $J\rightarrow J-1$

$$
\nu=\frac{E_J-E_{J-1}}{h}
$$

$$
\nu=\frac{\hbar^2J}{Ih}
$$

Using the given rotational constant

$$
\nu=2BcJ
$$

Thus, adjacent lines differ by

$$
\Delta\nu=2Bc
$$

$$
\Delta\nu=\frac{\hbar^2}{Ih}
$$

Since $\hbar=h/(2\pi)$

$$
\Delta\nu=\frac{h}{4\pi^2I}
$$

$$
\Delta\nu=\frac{6.6\times10^{-34}}{4\pi^2(2.70\times10^{-47})}\unit{Hz}
$$

### Final answer

$$
\boxed{\Delta\nu=6.2\times10^{11}\unit{Hz}}
$$

problem_statement:
Assume order-of-magnitude estimates for a diatomic molecule in Gaussian units, where Coulomb interactions scale as e^2/d. Symbols and definitions: d is the characteristic molecular linear size (of order a_0), p is the electron momentum uncertainty, ħ is the reduced Planck constant, e is the elementary charge magnitude, m_e is the electron mass, m is the reduced mass of the two nuclei, m_n is a typical nuclear mass, I is the molecular moment of inertia about its center of mass, f is the Coulomb force magnitude between nuclei, K is the force gradient (effective spring constant), ω is the angular frequency of nuclear vibration, Δx is the vibrational displacement amplitude. Energies: E_elect is the electronic excitation energy spacing, E_vib is the vibrational quantum, and E_rot is a typical rotational excitation energy. The Bohr radius is a_0, defined by a_0 = ħ^2/(m_e e^2). In part (b), an intermediate symbol E is used as an order-of-magnitude elastic constant with the same dimensions and scale as K; it is only a placeholder in the frequency estimate and should not be confused with the energies E_elect, E_vib, E_rot.

a) Using the fact that electrons in a molecule are confined to a volume typical of the molecule, estimate the spacing in energy of the excited states of the electrons (E_elect).

b) As nuclei in a molecule move they distort electronic wave functions. This distortion changes the electronic energy. The nuclei oscillate about positions of minimum total energy, comprising the electron energy and the repulsive Coulomb energy between nuclei. Estimate the frequency and therefore the energy of these vibrations (E_vib) by saying that a nucleus is in a harmonic oscillator potential.

c) Estimate the deviations from the equilibrium sites of the nuclei.

d) Estimate the energy of the rotational excitations (E_rot)

e) Estimate the ratio of E_elect:E_vib:E_rot in terms of the ratio of electron mass to nuclear mass, m_e / m_n
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 $$p d \approx \hbar$$
$$E_{elect} = \frac{p^2}{2 m_e}$$
$$E_{elect} \approx \frac{\hbar^2}{2 m_e d^2}$$
$$a_0 = \frac{\hbar^2}{m_e e^2}$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 $$f \approx \frac{e^2}{d^2}$$
$$K \approx \frac{f}{d}$$
$$K \approx \frac{e^2}{d^3}$$
$$\omega = \sqrt{\frac{E}{m}}$$
$$\omega \approx \sqrt{\frac{m_e}{m}} \sqrt{\frac{e^2 a_0}{m_e d^4}}$$
$$\omega = \sqrt{\frac{m_e}{m}} \frac{\hbar}{m_e d^2}$$
$$E_{vib} = \hbar \omega$$
$$E_{vib} \approx \sqrt{\frac{m_e}{m}} E_{elect}$$

Solution for subproblem(c):
 $$E_{vib} = \frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 (\Delta x)^2$$
$$E_{vib} = \hbar \omega$$
$$\Delta x \approx \left( \frac{m_e}{m} \right)^{\frac{1}{4}} d$$

Solution for subproblem(d):
 $$E_{rot} \approx \frac{\hbar^2}{2 I}$$
$$I \approx m d^2$$
$$E_{rot} \approx \frac{m_e}{m} E_{elect}$$

Solution for subproblem(e):
 $$m \approx m_n$$
$$E_{elect} : E_{vib} : E_{rot} \approx 1 : \sqrt{\frac{m_e}{m_n}} : \frac{m_e}{m_n}$$
model_response:
### a) Electronic excitation energy

Confinement over size $d$ gives

$$
pd\sim\hbar
$$

$$
p\sim\frac{\hbar}{d}
$$

The electronic kinetic-energy scale is

$$
E_{elect}\sim\frac{p^2}{m_e}
$$

$$
E_{elect}\sim\frac{\hbar^2}{m_ed^2}
$$

For $d\sim a_0$, the kinetic and Coulomb scales are comparable

$$
E_{elect}\sim\frac{e^2}{d}
$$

$$
E_{elect}\sim\frac{m_ee^4}{\hbar^2}
$$

### b) Vibrational excitation energy

The nuclear Coulomb force has scale

$$
f\sim\frac{e^2}{d^2}
$$

The effective spring constant is

$$
K\sim\frac{f}{d}
$$

$$
K\sim\frac{e^2}{d^3}
$$

The nuclear vibration frequency is

$$
\omega\sim\sqrt{\frac{K}{m}}
$$

$$
\omega\sim\sqrt{\frac{e^2}{md^3}}
$$

Thus

$$
E_{vib}\sim\hbar\omega
$$

$$
E_{vib}\sim\hbar\sqrt{\frac{e^2}{md^3}}
$$

Using $d\sim a_0$

$$
E_{vib}\sim E_{elect}\sqrt{\frac{m_e}{m}}
$$

### c) Nuclear displacement

For the harmonic-oscillator ground-state scale

$$
K\Delta x^2\sim\hbar\omega
$$

$$
\Delta x\sim\sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{m\omega}}
$$

Substituting the frequency estimate gives

$$
\frac{\Delta x}{d}\sim\left(\frac{\hbar^2}{me^2d}\right)^{1/4}
$$

For $d\sim a_0$

$$
\Delta x\sim d\left(\frac{m_e}{m}\right)^{1/4}
$$

### d) Rotational excitation energy

The molecular moment of inertia is

$$
I\sim md^2
$$

A typical rotational angular momentum is of order $\hbar$, so

$$
E_{rot}\sim\frac{\hbar^2}{I}
$$

$$
E_{rot}\sim\frac{\hbar^2}{md^2}
$$

For $d\sim a_0$

$$
E_{rot}\sim E_{elect}\frac{m_e}{m}
$$

### e) Final energy hierarchy

Since $m\sim m_n$ in order of magnitude

$$
\boxed{E_{elect}:E_{vib}:E_{rot}\sim1:\left(\frac{m_e}{m_n}\right)^{1/2}:\frac{m_e}{m_n}}
$$

The nuclear displacement scale is

$$
\boxed{\frac{\Delta x}{d}\sim\left(\frac{m_e}{m_n}\right)^{1/4}}
$$

AI_audit.reason: The model’s order-of-magnitude results are physically and algebraically equivalent to the valid reference: $K\sim e^2/d^3$ gives $\omega\sim\sqrt{e^2/(md^3)}$, and with $d\sim a_0=\hbar^2/(m_e e^2)$ this yields $E_{\mathrm{vib}}\sim E_{\mathrm{elect}}\sqrt{m_e/m}$, $\Delta x/d\sim (m_e/m)^{1/4}$, and $E_{\mathrm{rot}}\sim E_{\mathrm{elect}}(m_e/m)$. Hence for $m\sim m_n$ the hierarchy is $1:\sqrt{m_e/m_n}:m_e/m_n$. Differences such as omitted factors of $1/2$ are immaterial in an order-of-magnitude estimate.

problem_statement:
The size R of a nucleus can be determined by three types of measurements: (a) electron scattering, (b) energy levels of muonic atoms, and (c) ground state energies within an isotopic spin multiplet. Definitions used throughout: F(q^2) is the elastic nuclear form factor defined from the ratio of differential cross sections dσ_exp and dσ_point for experimental data and a pointlike nucleus, respectively; q is the momentum transfer and r is the position vector relative to the nuclear center; ρ(r) is the spherically symmetric nuclear charge density normalized to 1 with ⟨r^2⟩ = ∫ρ(r) r^2 d^3r the mean square charge radius; θ is the angle between q and r. In the muonic-atom method, m_μ is the muon mass, m_e is the electron mass, a_μ is the muonic Bohr radius, and a_0 is the electronic Bohr radius; H is the Hamiltonian, V(r) is the electrostatic potential, V_0(r) is the point-nucleus Coulomb potential, H′ = V − V_0 is the perturbation due to finite nuclear size, e is the elementary charge, Φ_0 is the 1s wavefunction for a point nucleus, ΔE is the ground-state energy shift, E_0 and E_1 are point-nucleus energy levels of the ground and first excited states, and E_X is the X-ray transition energy between these states. In the isotopic-multiplet method, M(Z,A) is the mass of a nucleus with proton number Z and mass number A, ΔE_e is the electromagnetic contribution to the mass difference, m_n and m_p are the neutron and proton masses, c is the speed of light, and R_0 is an empirical constant. All units, when shown, use \unit{}, e.g. \unit{fm} and \unit{cm}.

a) electron scattering,

b) energy levels of muonic atoms, or

c) ground state energies of the isotopic spin multiplet . Discuss what physical quantities are measured in two and only two of these three experiments and how these quantities are related to the radius of the nucleus.
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 The measured quantity is the elastic nuclear form factor obtained from the ratio of differential cross sections
$$F(q^2)=\frac{(d\sigma)_{exp}}{(d\sigma)_{point}}$$
In the first Born approximation
$$F(q^2)=\int \rho(r) e^{i q\cdot r} d^3 r$$
Assuming spherical symmetry ρ(r)=ρ(r) and small momentum transfer q\cdot r \ll 1, expand the exponential and keep terms to order q^2
$$F(q^2)\approx\int \rho(r)\bigl[1-\tfrac{1}{2}(q\cdot r)^2\bigr] d^3 r$$
Carrying out the angular average gives
$$F(q^2)=1-\frac{1}{6} q^2\langle r^2\rangle$$
with the mean square radius defined by
$$\langle r^2\rangle=\int \rho(r) r^2 d^3 r$$
By measuring the angular distribution of elastically scattered electrons one determines F(q^2), and by inversion obtains ρ(r) and hence the nuclear size.

Solution for subproblem(b):
 The measured quantities are the transition energies between muonic-atom levels, which are highly sensitive to the finite nuclear radius because m_\mu \approx 210 m_ e and a_\mu \approx \frac{1}{210} a_0. For an s state the Hamiltonian is
$$H=-\frac{1}{2 m_\mu} \nabla^2+V(r)$$
For a pointlike nucleus
$$V_0(r)=-\frac{e^2}{r}$$
For a uniformly charged sphere of radius R, inside the nucleus one has
$$V(r)=-\frac{e^2}{2 R^3}\bigl(3 R^2-r^2\bigr)$$
for 0<r\le R, and outside the nucleus
$$V(r)=-\frac{e^2}{r}$$
for r>R. The perturbation due to finite size is H′=V−V_0. Inside the nucleus
$$H'= -\frac{e^2}{2 R^3}\bigl(3 R^2-r^2\bigr)+\frac{e^2}{r}$$
for 0<r\le R, and outside the nucleus
$$H'=0$$
for r>R. The ground-state energy shift is
$$\Delta E=\langle \Phi_0\vert H'\vert \Phi_0\rangle$$
which gives
$$\Delta E=4\pi \int_0^R |\Phi_0|^2 H' r^2 dr$$
with the 1s wavefunction
$$\Phi_0=\bigl(\frac{1}{\pi a_\mu^3}\bigr)^{1/2} e^{-r/a_\mu}$$
Since R\sim 10^{-12} \unit{cm} and a_\mu\sim 10^{-10} \unit{cm}, we have
$$\frac{R}{a_\mu}\ll 1$$
and therefore
$$e^{-2 r/a_\mu}\approx 1-\frac{2 r}{a_\mu}$$
Keeping terms up to order (R/a_\mu)^2 yields
$$\Delta E=\frac{2}{5}\bigl(\frac{e^2}{2 a_\mu}\bigr)\bigl(\frac{R}{a_\mu}\bigr)^2$$
The X-ray energy for the transition from the first excited state to the ground state is then
$$E_X=(E_1-E_0)-\frac{2}{5}\bigl(\frac{e^2}{a_\mu}\bigr)\bigl(\frac{R}{a_\mu}\bigr)^2$$
where E_1 and E_0 are the point-nucleus energy levels of the first excited and ground states. Given E_X and E_1-E_0, the radius R can be deduced.

Solution for subproblem(c):
 For nuclei within the same isotopic spin multiplet, the strong-interaction structure is the same, so mass differences arise from electromagnetic interactions and the proton–neutron mass difference. Define the measured mass-energy difference
$$\Delta E=[M(Z,A)-M(Z-1,A)] c^2$$
This can be written as
$$\Delta E=\Delta E_e-(m_n-m_p) c^2$$
The electromagnetic contribution for a uniformly charged sphere of radius R is
$$\Delta E_e=\frac{3 e^2}{5 R}\bigl[Z^2-(Z-1)^2\bigr]$$
From these relations R is deduced. Empirically one finds
$$R\approx R_0 A^{1/3}$$
with
$$R_0=1.2-1.4 \unit{fm}$$
model_response:
### Method (a): Electron scattering

The measured differential cross-section ratio gives the elastic form factor

$$
F(q^2)^2=\frac{d\sigma_{\exp}/d\Omega}{d\sigma_{\rm point}/d\Omega}
$$

For a spherical charge distribution

$$
F(q^2)=\int \rho(r)\cos(qr\cos\theta)d^3r
$$

At small momentum transfer

$$
\cos(qr\cos\theta)\simeq1-\frac{q^2r^2\cos^2\theta}{2}
$$

Spherical averaging gives

$$
\langle\cos^2\theta\rangle=\frac{1}{3}
$$

Therefore

$$
F(q^2)\simeq1-\frac{q^2\langle r^2\rangle}{6}
$$

Hence the measured slope at $q^2=0$ determines the mean-square charge radius

$$
\langle r^2\rangle=-6\frac{dF}{d(q^2)}\bigg|_{q^2=0}
$$

The nuclear rms charge radius is

$$
R=\sqrt{\langle r^2\rangle}
$$

### Method (b): Muonic-atom energy levels

The finite-size perturbation is

$$
H'=V(r)-V_0(r)
$$

The ground-state energy shift is

$$
\Delta E=\int |\Phi_0(r)|^2H'd^3r
$$

Since the nucleus is much smaller than the muonic orbit, $R\ll a_\mu$

$$
|\Phi_0(r)|^2\simeq|\Phi_0(0)|^2
$$

For the point-nucleus $1s$ state

$$
|\Phi_0(0)|^2=\frac{1}{\pi a_\mu^3}
$$

The leading finite-size shift is

$$
\Delta E=\frac{2\pi Ze^2}{3}|\Phi_0(0)|^2\langle r^2\rangle
$$

Thus

$$
\Delta E=\frac{2Ze^2}{3a_\mu^3}\langle r^2\rangle
$$

The measured X-ray transition energy is approximately

$$
E_X=E_1-E_0-\Delta E
$$

Therefore

$$
\Delta E=E_1-E_0-E_X
$$

The nuclear radius follows from

$$
R=\sqrt{\frac{3a_\mu^3\Delta E}{2Ze^2}}
$$

The enhanced sensitivity results from

$$
a_\mu\simeq a_0\frac{m_e}{m_\mu}
$$

### Final answer

In electron scattering, the measured quantity is the cross-section ratio, which determines the low-$q^2$ slope of $F(q^2)$ and hence $R$. In muonic atoms, the measured quantity is the X-ray transition energy $E_X$, whose finite-size shift $\Delta E$ is proportional to $R^2$.

AI_audit.reason: The reference conflates the form-factor amplitude with the cross-section ratio: physically, (dσ_exp/dσ_point)=|F(q²)|², with F=1−q²⟨r²⟩/6+…, whereas the reference defines the ratio itself as F but still uses the amplitude’s 1/6 slope. Its muonic result is also internally inconsistent by a factor of two: for a uniform sphere, ΔE=(2/5)Ze²R_geom²/a_μ³=(2Ze²/3a_μ³)⟨r²⟩, matching the model, while the reference first writes only (1/5)e²R²/a_μ³ and later uses 2/5. Thus the benchmark/reference is materially invalid.

problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) A nucleus with nuclear g-factor g and mass m_N undergoes Larmor precession in the Earth's magnetic field B. In Gaussian-cgs units, the precession angular frequency is given by omega = g e B / (2 m_N c), where e is the elementary charge and c is the speed of light. Use the order-of-magnitude values g = 1, e = 4.8 × 10^{-10} esu, c = 3 × 10^{10} cm/s, B ≈ 0.5 Gs, and m_N ≈ 10^{-23} g for a light nucleus. Estimate omega and select the closest option among 10^{-1}, 10^{1}, 10^{3}, 10^{5} s^{-1}. State the final answer as omega in s^{-1}.
reference_solution:
The precession angular frequency is
$$
\omega = \frac{g e B}{2 m_N c}
$$
Given
$$
g = 1
$$
$$
e = 4.8 \times 10^{-10} \unit{esu}
$$
$$
c = 3 \times 10^{10} \unit{cm/s}
$$
$$
B = 0.5 \unit{Gs}
$$
$$
m_N = 10^{-23} \unit{g}

$$
\omega = \frac{4.8 \times 0.5 \times 10^{-10}}{2 \times 10^{-23} \times 3 \times 10^{10}} \unit{s^{-1}}
$$
Evaluating the powers and numerical factors yields
$$
\omega = 0.4 \times 10^{3} \unit{s^{-1}}
$$
Thus, the closest option is
$$
\omega = 10^{3} \unit{s^{-1}}
$$

The Larmor angular frequency is

problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) The nucleus ^{27}_{14}Si decays to its mirror nucleus ^{27}_{13}Al by positron emission. The decay is ^{27}_{14}Si -> ^{27}_{13}Al + beta^+ + nu, where beta^+ denotes the positron and nu denotes the neutrino. The maximum total positron energy E_{pos,max}, defined as kinetic energy plus m_e c^2, is 3.48 MeV. Neglect the recoil energy of the daughter nucleus. Assume that the mass-energy difference between the initial and final nuclei is entirely due to the Coulomb energy. Model each nucleus as a uniformly charged sphere with total charge Z e and radius R, where Z is the atomic number and e is the elementary charge. Assume the nuclear radius satisfies R = r_0 A^{1/3}, where A is the mass number and r_0 is a constant to be estimated. Let m_e be the electron mass, c the speed of light, and hbar the reduced Planck constant. Define E_e as the Coulomb energy difference between the two nuclei, computed from the uniform-sphere model. For numerical evaluation, use e^2 = hbar c / 137 and hbar c = 197 \unit{MeV fm}.
model_response:
### Step 1: Coulomb energy

For a uniformly charged sphere,

$$
U(Z)=\frac{3Z^2e^2}{5R}
$$

Thus,

$$
E_e=U(14)-U(13)
$$

$$
E_e=\frac{3e^2}{5R}(14^2-13^2)
$$

$$
E_e=\frac{81e^2}{5R}
$$

### Step 2: Endpoint energy

At the endpoint, the neutrino energy is zero. Since the positron energy includes its rest energy,

$$
E_{\mathrm{pos,max}}=K_{\mathrm{pos,max}}+m_ec^2
$$

Neglecting nuclear recoil,

$$
E_e=E_{\mathrm{pos,max}}
$$

$$
E_e=3.48\unit{MeV}
$$

### Step 3: Nuclear radius

Using $R=r_0A^{1/3}$ and $27^{1/3}=3$,

$$
R=3r_0
$$

Also,

$$
e^2=\frac{197\unit{MeV fm}}{137}
$$

$$
e^2=1.438\unit{MeV fm}
$$

Therefore,

$$
r_0=\frac{3(14^2-13^2)(1.438\unit{MeV fm})}{5(3)(3.48\unit{MeV})}
$$

### Final answer

$$
\boxed{r_0\approx2.23\unit{fm}}
$$

The corresponding nuclear radius is

$$
\boxed{R\approx6.69\unit{fm}}
$$

AI_audit.reason: The reference adds an erroneous positron rest-mass term. Since E_e is explicitly the initial–final nuclear mass-energy difference and E_pos,max is the positron’s total energy, endpoint conservation gives E_e=E_pos,max=3.48 MeV, not E_pos,max+2m_ec^2. Thus r_0=27e^2/(5E_e)≈2.23 fm, exactly the model’s result; the materially incorrect reference makes this a benchmark failure.

problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) Discuss thermonuclear reactions. Provide concrete examples of reactions important in the Sun, in the H bomb (uncontrolled thermonuclear reaction), and in controlled fusion attempts. Estimate, in electron volts per reaction, the energy release for each example. Also describe the most important characteristic of the nuclear force relevant to these reactions. Notation and definitions to be used in the solution: p denotes a proton, d denotes a deuteron (2H), t denotes a triton (3H), n denotes a neutron, 3He and 4He denote helium-3 and helium-4, respectively, 6Li denotes lithium-6, e^{+} denotes a positron, ν_e denotes an electron neutrino, and γ denotes a gamma ray. The quantity Q denotes the energy released per reaction. M(X) denotes the atomic mass of nuclide X, and c denotes the speed of light. Energies are expressed in eV (specifically MeV) and masses in amu, with units written using \unit{}.
reference_solution:
In the Sun, the dominant thermonuclear process is the proton–proton chain:

$$
p + p \to d + e^{+} + \nu_e
$$

$$
d + p \to {}^{3}He + \gamma
$$

$$
{}^{3}He + {}^{3}He \to {}^{4}He + 2 p
$$

The net reaction is

$$
4 p \to {}^{4}He + 2 e^{+} + 2 \nu_e
$$

The energy release for the net reaction is

$$
Q = [4 M({}^{1}H) - M({}^{4}He)] c^{2}
$$

$$
4 \times 1.008142 - 4.003860
$$

$$
0.02871 \unit{amu}
$$

$$
26.9 \unit{MeV}
$$

In an H bomb, an uncontrolled thermonuclear reaction uses a condensed mixture typically containing deuterium, tritium, and lithium. A representative reaction chain is

$$
{}^{6}Li + n \to {}^{4}He + t
$$

$$
d + t \to {}^{4}He + n
$$

The resulting net reaction is

$$
{}^{6}Li + d \to 2 \cdot {}^{4}He
$$

The energy released per reaction is

$$
Q = [M({}^{6}Li) + M({}^{2}H) - 2 M({}^{4}He)] c^{2}
$$

$$
6.01690 + 2.01471 - 2 \times 4.00388
$$

$$
0.02385 \unit{amu}
$$

$$
22.4 \unit{MeV}
$$

An example of a possible controlled fusion reaction is

$$
t + d \to {}^{4}He + n
$$

The corresponding energy release is

$$
Q = [M({}^{3}H) + M({}^{2}H) - M({}^{4}He) - M(n)] c^{2}
$$

$$
3.01695 + 2.01471 - 4.00388 - 1.00896
$$

$$
0.01882 \unit{amu}
$$

$$
17.65 \unit{MeV}
$$

The most important characteristic of the nuclear force in these reactions is saturation: a nucleon interacts strongly only with nearby nucleons. As a result, nucleons in the interior of a nucleus have their interactions saturated, whereas those on the surface do not. Because lighter nuclei have a larger surface-to-volume ratio, their mean binding energy per nucleon is smaller than that of medium-mass nuclei, indicating looser binding. For very heavy nuclei, however, the Coulomb repulsion among protons reduces the mean binding energy per nucleon relative to medium-mass nuclei.
model_response:
### 1. Thermonuclear reactions

Thermonuclear fusion joins light nuclei at very high temperature. Thermal motion and quantum tunneling allow nuclei to penetrate the Coulomb barrier.

The nuclear force is extremely strong and attractive but has a short range of approximately $1\unit{fm}$. Energy is released because the fusion products have greater binding energy per nucleon.

### 2. Fusion in the Sun

The proton-proton chain begins with

$$
p+p\rightarrow d+e^{+}+\nu_e
$$

$$
Q\approx0.42\unit{MeV}
$$

The deuteron then captures a proton

$$
d+p\rightarrow{}^3He+\gamma
$$

$$
Q\approx5.49\unit{MeV}
$$

The main branch ends with

$$
{}^3He+{}^3He\rightarrow{}^4He+2p
$$

$$
Q\approx12.86\unit{MeV}
$$

The net reaction, including positron annihilation, is

$$
4p\rightarrow{}^4He+2e^{+}+2\nu_e
$$

Using atomic masses,

$$
Q=[4M({}^1H)-M({}^4He)]c^2
$$

$$
Q\approx26.7\unit{MeV}
$$

Thus the gross energy release is

$$
Q\approx2.67\times10^7\unit{eV}
$$

A small fraction is carried away by the neutrinos.

### 3. Hydrogen bomb

A principal uncontrolled fusion reaction is deuterium-tritium fusion

$$
d+t\rightarrow{}^4He+n
$$

$$
Q=[M(d)+M(t)-M({}^4He)-M(n)]c^2
$$

$$
Q\approx17.6\unit{MeV}
$$

$$
Q\approx1.76\times10^7\unit{eV}
$$

Lithium-6 can generate tritium through neutron capture

$$
{}^6Li+n\rightarrow{}^4He+t
$$

$$
Q\approx4.78\unit{MeV}
$$

$$
Q\approx4.78\times10^6\unit{eV}
$$

### 4. Controlled fusion attempts

The most common proposed reactor reaction is also

$$
d+t\rightarrow{}^4He+n
$$

$$
Q\approx17.6\unit{MeV}
$$

The alpha particle receives approximately

$$
Q_{{}^4He}\approx3.5\unit{MeV}
$$

The neutron receives approximately

$$
Q_n\approx14.1\unit{MeV}
$$

A possible lower-neutron alternative is

$$
d+{}^3He\rightarrow{}^4He+p
$$

$$
Q\approx18.3\unit{MeV}
$$

$$
Q\approx1.83\times10^7\unit{eV}
$$

### Final answer

Thermonuclear reactions require temperatures high enough for light nuclei to approach within the short range of the attractive nuclear force. The representative releases are

$$
Q_{\rm Sun}\approx26.7\unit{MeV}
$$

$$
Q_{d+t}\approx17.6\unit{MeV}
$$

$$
Q_{{}^6Li+n}\approx4.78\unit{MeV}
$$

$$
Q_{d+{}^3He}\approx18.3\unit{MeV}
$$

AI_audit.reason: The response is physically correct: it gives valid thermonuclear examples with standard Q values (pp-chain net ≈26.7 MeV, D–T ≈17.6 MeV, 6Li+n ≈4.78 MeV, and D–3He ≈18.3 MeV). The H-bomb examples need not be combined into the reference’s 6Li+d net reaction; their Q values sum to the same ≈22.4 MeV chain release. Its identification of the nuclear force’s ~1 fm short range—so nucleons interact chiefly with nearby nucleons—is the physical basis of the reference’s saturation property, even though it does not use that term.

problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) A recent model for collective nuclear states treats them in terms of interacting bosons. Consider states that are fully symmetric superpositions of S bosons and D bosons. Each S boson has spin 0, and each D boson has spin 2. Let N_s denote the number of S bosons and N_d denote the number of D bosons. Let E_s be the single-boson energy of each S boson and E_d be the single-boson energy of each D boson. There is a residual interaction of constant strength alpha between each distinct pair of D bosons, contributing alpha per D–D pair. Let J denote the total spin of a state, and let J_{N_d,k} denote the k-th allowed value of J for a given N_d, ordered from smallest to largest. Determine the allowed total spins for N_d = 0, 1, 2, 3. Then, for all configurations with fixed total boson number N_s + N_d = 3, determine the total energy E of each configuration.
model_response:
### Allowed total spins

Fully symmetric coupling of spin-0 and spin-2 bosons gives

$$
J_{0,k}\in\{0\}
$$

$$
J_{1,k}\in\{2\}
$$

$$
J_{2,k}\in\{0,2,4\}
$$

$$
J_{3,k}\in\{0,2,3,4,6\}
$$

### Energy formula

The number of distinct D–D pairs is

$$
\frac{N_d(N_d-1)}{2}
$$

Therefore

$$
E=N_sE_s+N_dE_d+\alpha\frac{N_d(N_d-1)}{2}
$$

For $N_s+N_d=3$:

$$
E(3,0,J=0)=3E_s
$$

$$
E(2,1,J=2)=2E_s+E_d
$$

$$
E(1,2,J\in\{0,2,4\})=E_s+2E_d+\alpha
$$

$$
E(0,3,J\in\{0,2,3,4,6\})=3E_d+3\alpha
$$

AI_audit.reason: The reference solution incorrectly omits $J=3$ for three fully symmetric spin-2 bosons. Indeed, $\mathrm{Sym}^{3}(V_2)=V_6\oplus V_4\oplus V_3\oplus V_2\oplus V_0$ (dimensions $13+9+7+5+1=35$), so the model’s $N_d=3$ set $\{0,2,3,4,6\}$ is correct. Its pair-counting energy $E=N_sE_s+N_dE_d+\alpha N_d(N_d-1)/2$ also reproduces all listed energies.

problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) Let \sigma denote the total scattering cross-section for low-energy neutron–nucleus scattering, measured in \unit{cm^2}. Let r denote the radius of the sphere of action of nuclear forces, measured in \unit{cm}. Choose the typical value of \sigma from the following options: 10^{-16} \unit{cm^2}, 10^{-24} \unit{cm^2}, 10^{-32} \unit{cm^2}, 10^{-40} \unit{cm^2}.

$$\sigma \sim \pi r^2$$
This corresponds to the option 10^{-24} \unit{cm^2}
$$\sigma = 10^{-24} \unit{cm^2}$$

Low-energy neutron–nucleus scattering cross-sections are typically of the order of one barn

$$

$$

Thus

$$
\sigma\sim10^{-24}\unit{cm^2}
$$

### Final Answer

$$
\boxed{\sigma=10^{-24}\unit{cm^2}}
$$

problem_statement:
Calculate the ratio R for e^+ e^- -> hadrons at leading order (ignoring QCD and quark-mass effects). Define R = sigma(e^+ e^- -> hadrons) / sigma(e^+ e^- -> mu^+ mu^-). Let N_c = 3 be the number of QCD colors. Let Q_i be the electric charge (in units of e) of the quark flavor i that is kinematically accessible at the given center-of-mass energy. Use the leading-order expression R = N_c * sum_i Q_i^2. Compute R in the specified energy ranges.

a) just below the threshold for “charm” production,

b) above that threshold but below the $b$ quark production threshold.
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 At this energy, the accessible quark flavors are u, d, and s, with charges Q_u = 2/3 and Q_d = Q_s = -1/3.
$$R = 3 \sum_{i} Q_i^2$$
For these flavors:
$$\sum_{i=u,d,s} Q_i^2 = \frac{4}{9} + \frac{1}{9} + \frac{1}{9}$$
$$\sum_{i=u,d,s} Q_i^2 = \frac{2}{3}$$
$$R = 2$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 At this energy, the accessible quark flavors are u, d, s, and c, with Q_c = 2/3.
$$R = 3 \sum_{i} Q_i^2$$
For these flavors:
$$\sum_{i=u,d,s,c} Q_i^2 = \frac{4}{9} + \frac{1}{9} + \frac{1}{9} + \frac{4}{9}$$
$$\sum_{i=u,d,s,c} Q_i^2 = \frac{10}{9}$$
$$R = \frac{10}{3}$$
model_response:
### Leading-order expression

$$R=N_c\sum_i Q_i^2$$

$$N_c=3$$

### a) Below the charm threshold

Accessible flavors: $u,d,s$

$$Q_u=\frac{2}{3}$$

$$Q_d=Q_s=-\frac{1}{3}$$

$$\sum_i Q_i^2=\frac{4}{9}+\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{9}=\frac{2}{3}$$

$$R=3\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)$$

$$\boxed{R=2}$$

### b) Above the charm threshold but below the bottom threshold

Accessible flavors: $u,d,s,c$

$$Q_c=\frac{2}{3}$$

$$\sum_i Q_i^2=\frac{4}{9}+\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{9}+\frac{4}{9}=\frac{10}{9}$$

$$R=3\left(\frac{10}{9}\right)$$

$$\boxed{R=\frac{10}{3}}$$

problem_statement:
The bag model of hadron structure has colored quarks moving as independent spin-half Dirac particles within a spherical cavity of radius R. To obtain wave functions for particular hadron states, the individual quark orbitals must be combined to produce states of zero total color and the appropriate values of the spin and flavor (isospin, charge, strangeness) quantum numbers. In the approximation that the up and down quarks are massless, the lowest energy s-wave bag orbitals are given by the Dirac spinor
$$
\psi = N \begin{pmatrix} j_0(k r)\, \chi \\ i j_1(k r)\, \sigma \cdot \hat s\, \chi \end{pmatrix}
$$
where N is a normalization constant, j_l is the spherical Bessel function, σ denotes the Pauli matrices, χ is a 2-component Pauli spinor, s is the position vector, r is the radial coordinate r = |s|, and \hat s = s / r is the radial unit vector. The wave number k is fixed by the bag boundary condition
$$
k = \frac{2.04}{R}
$$
Color labels are denoted by R, G, B. The single-quark electric charge eigenvalues (in units of the proton charge e) are defined by
$$
Q_u = \frac{2}{3}
$$
$$
Q_d = -\frac{1}{3}
$$
The total magnetic moment operator is defined by
$$
\mu = \int_{|s|<R} \frac{1}{2} s \times J_{EM} \; d^3 s
$$
where J_{EM} is the usual Dirac electromagnetic current for a single quark with charge eigenvalue Q in {\frac{2}{3}, -\frac{1}{3}}

a) The lowest-lying baryons (proton and neutron) are obtained by putting three quarks in this orbital. How would you construct the wave function for the proton and for the neutron, i.e., which quarks would be combined and what is the structure of the spin wave function consistent with the quantum numbers of proton and neutron and Pauli’s principle?

b) The magnetic moment operator is defined as μ = ∫_{|s|<R} (1/2) s × J_EM d^3 s, where J_EM is the usual Dirac electric current operator. Find an expression for this operator in terms of the spin operators of the constituent quarks. You may leave integrals over Bessel functions undone.

c) Show that μ_n / μ_p = -2/3. You may need the following Clebsch–Gordon coefficients:
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 Neglecting color, the lowest states of a baryon are symmetric under exchange of any two quarks. The third component of isospin for the proton is I_3 = \frac{1}{2}, while u has I_3 = \frac{1}{2} and d has I_3 = -\frac{1}{2}, so the proton’s quark content is uud. Since the total isospin is \frac{1}{2}, the flavor part cannot be completely symmetric under u \leftrightarrow d exchange; thus it must contain components of the form uud − udu. To maintain overall symmetry, multiply this by a spin wave function antisymmetric under exchange of the corresponding quarks. A convenient spin-up building block under exchange of quarks 2 and 3 is
$$
\nu_1 = u\uparrow(1)\, u\uparrow(2)\, d\downarrow(3) - u\uparrow(1)\, d\uparrow(2)\, u\downarrow(3)
$$
Exchanging the first and second quarks gives
$$
\nu_2 = u\uparrow\, u\uparrow\, d\downarrow - d\uparrow\, u\uparrow\, u\downarrow - u\downarrow\, u\uparrow\, d\uparrow + d\downarrow\, u\uparrow\, u\uparrow
$$
Exchanging the first and third quarks gives
$$
\nu_3 = d\downarrow\, u\uparrow\, u\uparrow - u\downarrow\, d\uparrow\, u\uparrow - d\uparrow\, u\downarrow\, u\uparrow + u\uparrow\, d\downarrow\, u\uparrow
$$
Combining and normalizing, the totally symmetric spin-flavor wave function for a spin-up proton is
$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{18}}\big( 2\, u\uparrow\, u\uparrow\, d\downarrow + 2\, u\uparrow\, d\downarrow\, u\uparrow + 2\, d\downarrow\, u\uparrow\, u\uparrow - u\uparrow\, u\downarrow\, d\uparrow - u\uparrow\, d\uparrow\, u\downarrow - u\downarrow\, u\uparrow\, d\uparrow - u\downarrow\, d\uparrow\, u\uparrow - d\uparrow\, u\uparrow\, u\downarrow - d\uparrow\, u\downarrow\, u\uparrow \big)
$$
The totally antisymmetric color wave function is
$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\big( RGB - RBG + GBR - GRB + BRG - BGR \big)
$$
Introduce the s-wave spinor orbitals
$$
\psi_{\uparrow} = \begin{pmatrix} j_0(k r)\, \chi(\uparrow) \\ i j_1(k r)\, \sigma \cdot \hat s\, \chi(\uparrow) \end{pmatrix}
$$
$$
\chi(\uparrow) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}
$$
$$
\psi_{\downarrow} = \begin{pmatrix} j_0(k r)\, \chi(\downarrow) \\ i j_1(k r)\, \sigma \cdot \hat s\, \chi(\downarrow) \end{pmatrix}
$$
$$
\chi(\downarrow) = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}
$$
Promote each spin arrow to the corresponding orbital spinor to obtain the spin-up proton state
$$
\frac{1}{6\sqrt{3}}\big( RGB - RBG + GBR - GRB + BRG - BGR \big) \Big( 2\, u\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\downarrow} + 2\, u\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\downarrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow} + 2\, d\psi_{\downarrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow} - u\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\downarrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow} - u\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\downarrow} - u\psi_{\downarrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow} - u\psi_{\downarrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow} - d\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\downarrow} - d\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\downarrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow} \Big)
$$
The spin-up neutron state is obtained by the isospin flip u \leftrightarrow d acting on the proton state
$$
\frac{1}{6\sqrt{3}}\big( RGB - RBG + GBR - GRB + BRG - BGR \big) \Big( 2\, d\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\downarrow} + 2\, d\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\downarrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow} + 2\, u\psi_{\downarrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow} - d\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\downarrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow} - d\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\downarrow} - d\psi_{\downarrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow} - d\psi_{\downarrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow} - u\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\downarrow} - u\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\downarrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow} \Big)
$$
For spin-down nucleons, interchange \uparrow and \downarrow in the above spin-up wave functions

Solution for subproblem(b):
 For a single quark with charge eigenvalue Q, the Dirac current is
$$
J_{EM} = Q \psi^{\dagger} \alpha \psi
$$
with
$$
\alpha = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \sigma \\ \sigma & 0 \end{pmatrix}
$$
Inserting the s-wave spinor gives
$$
J_{EM} = 2 Q |N|^2 j_0(k r) j_1(k r) \chi^{\dagger} ( \sigma \times \hat s ) \chi
$$
The magnetic moment operator is
$$
\mu = \int_{|s|<R} \frac{1}{2} s \times J_{EM} \; d^3 s
$$
Using the vector triple product and integrating over angles, the second term vanishes and we obtain
$$
\mu = 4 \pi Q |N|^2 \Big[ \int_0^R r^3 j_0(k r) j_1(k r) dr \Big] \chi^{\dagger} \sigma \chi
$$

Solution for subproblem(c):
 The Clebsch–Gordon coefficients are
$$
\langle 1/2, 1/2 \mid 1, 1; 1/2, 1/2 \rangle = \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}
$$
$$
\langle 1/2, 1/2 \mid 1, 0; 1/2, 1/2 \rangle = - \sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}
$$
Let the common positive factor be
$$
C = 4 \pi |N|^2 \int_0^R r^3 j_0(k r) j_1(k r) dr
$$
The expectation value of the proton magnetic moment for the spin-up state is
$$
\langle p\uparrow \mid \mu \mid p\uparrow \rangle = \frac{C}{18} \Big[ 4 \Big( \frac{2}{3} + \frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{3} \Big) + 4 \Big( \frac{2}{3} + \frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{3} \Big) + 4 \Big( \frac{2}{3} + \frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{3} \Big) + \Big( \frac{2}{3} - \frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{3} \Big) + \Big( \frac{2}{3} - \frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{3} \Big) + \Big( \frac{2}{3} - \frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{3} \Big) + \Big( \frac{2}{3} - \frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{3} \Big) + \Big( \frac{2}{3} - \frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{3} \Big) + \Big( \frac{2}{3} - \frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{3} \Big) \Big]
$$
$$
\langle p\uparrow \mid \mu \mid p\uparrow \rangle = C
$$
Similarly, for the spin-up neutron
$$
\langle n\uparrow \mid \mu \mid n\uparrow \rangle = \frac{C}{18} \Big[ 3 \times 4 \Big( -\frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{3} - \frac{2}{3} \Big) + 6 \Big( -\frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{3} - \frac{2}{3} \Big) \Big]
$$
$$
\langle n\uparrow \mid \mu \mid n\uparrow \rangle = - \frac{2}{3} C
$$
Therefore the ratio is
$$
\frac{\mu_n}{\mu_p} = - \frac{2}{3}
$$
model_response:
### a) Proton and neutron wave functions

The spatial state $\Phi_0$ is symmetric because all three quarks occupy the lowest orbital

$$
\Phi_0=\prod_{a=1}^{3}\psi_0(\vec s_a)
$$

Pauli’s principle therefore requires an antisymmetric color state and a symmetric spin-flavor state

$$
|C_A\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt6}(|RGB\rangle-|RBG\rangle+|GBR\rangle-|GRB\rangle+|BRG\rangle-|BGR\rangle)
$$

For spin projection $+\frac12$, the proton spin-flavor state is

$$
|p^\uparrow\rangle_{SF}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{18}}(2|u^\uparrow u^\uparrow d^\downarrow\rangle-|u^\uparrow u^\downarrow d^\uparrow\rangle-|u^\downarrow u^\uparrow d^\uparrow\rangle+2|u^\uparrow d^\downarrow u^\uparrow\rangle-|u^\uparrow d^\uparrow u^\downarrow\rangle-|u^\downarrow d^\uparrow u^\uparrow\rangle+2|d^\downarrow u^\uparrow u^\uparrow\rangle-|d^\uparrow u^\uparrow u^\downarrow\rangle-|d^\uparrow u^\downarrow u^\uparrow\rangle)
$$

The neutron state follows by interchanging $u$ and $d$

$$
|n^\uparrow\rangle_{SF}=|p^\uparrow\rangle_{SF}\big|_{u\leftrightarrow d}
$$

Thus

$$
|\Psi_{p^\uparrow}\rangle=\Phi_0|C_A\rangle|p^\uparrow\rangle_{SF}
$$

$$
|\Psi_{n^\uparrow}\rangle=\Phi_0|C_A\rangle|n^\uparrow\rangle_{SF}
$$

The two identical quarks form a spin-one pair, coupled to the remaining quark as

$$
\left|\frac12,\frac12\right\rangle=\sqrt{\frac23}|1,1\rangle|\downarrow\rangle-\sqrt{\frac13}|1,0\rangle|\uparrow\rangle
$$

The spin-down baryons follow by reversing all spin projections.

### b) Magnetic moment operator

For one quark of charge $eQ$, the current is

$$
\vec J_Q=eQ\psi^\dagger\vec\alpha\psi
$$

Substitution of the bag spinor gives

$$
\vec J_Q=2eQN^2j_0(kr)j_1(kr)(\vec\sigma\times\hat s)
$$

The angular integral needed in the magnetic moment is

$$
\int d\Omega[\vec\sigma-\hat s(\hat s\cdot\vec\sigma)]=\frac{8\pi}{3}\vec\sigma
$$

Hence the single-quark magnetic moment is

$$
\vec\mu_Q=\frac{8\pi eQN^2}{3}\vec\sigma\int_0^Rr^3j_0(kr)j_1(kr)dr
$$

Using $\vec S=\vec\sigma/2$, the three-quark operator becomes

$$
\vec\mu=C\sum_{a=1}^{3}Q_a\vec S_a
$$

where

$$
C=\frac{16\pi eN^2}{3}\int_0^Rr^3j_0(kr)j_1(kr)dr
$$

The normalization condition is

$$
N^{-2}=4\pi\int_0^Rr^2[j_0^2(kr)+j_1^2(kr)]dr
$$

Therefore

$$
C=\frac{4e}{3}\frac{\int_0^Rr^3j_0(kr)j_1(kr)dr}{\int_0^Rr^2[j_0^2(kr)+j_1^2(kr)]dr}
$$

with

$$
k=\frac{2.04}{R}
$$

### c) Magnetic-moment ratio

For the spin-up proton wave function

$$
\left\langle\sum_{u}\sigma_z\right\rangle_p=\frac43
$$

$$
\left\langle\sum_{d}\sigma_z\right\rangle_p=-\frac13
$$

Thus

$$
\mu_p=\frac{C}{2}\left[Q_u\frac43+Q_d\left(-\frac13\right)\right]
$$

$$
\mu_p=\frac{C}{2}
$$

For the neutron, the $u$ and $d$ spin contributions are interchanged

$$
\left\langle\sum_{u}\sigma_z\right\rangle_n=-\frac13
$$

$$
\left\langle\sum_{d}\sigma_z\right\rangle_n=\frac43
$$

Therefore

$$
\mu_n=\frac{C}{2}\left[Q_u\left(-\frac13\right)+Q_d\frac43\right]
$$

$$
\mu_n=-\frac{C}{3}
$$

problem_statement:
A relativistic particle of rest mass m_0 and kinetic energy 2 m_0 c^2 strikes and sticks to a stationary particle of rest mass 2 m_0. Let c denote the speed of light. Let p denote the magnitude of the three-momentum. Let S denote the invariant mass squared of the two-particle system. Let M denote the rest mass of the composite particle. Let \beta=v/c and \gamma=1/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}. In intermediate steps, adopt natural units with c=1; reinstate c when reporting the velocity.

a) Find the rest mass of the composite.

b) Find its velocity.
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 The moving particle has total energy 3 m_0 in natural units.

$$p=\sqrt{(3 m_0)^2-m_0^2}$$

$$p=\sqrt{8}\,m_0$$

$$S=(3 m_0+2 m_0)^2-p^2$$

$$S=17 m_0^2$$

Let the rest mass of the composite particle be M. Its momentum equals p by momentum conservation.

$$S=(\sqrt{M^2+p^2})^2-p^2$$

$$S=M^2$$

$$M=\sqrt{S}$$

$$M=\sqrt{17}\,m_0$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 For the composite particle, using p and M from part (a):

$$\gamma\beta=\frac{p}{M}$$

$$\gamma\beta=\sqrt{\frac{8}{17}}$$

$$\gamma=\sqrt{\gamma^2\beta^2+1}$$

$$\gamma=\sqrt{\frac{8}{17}+1}$$

$$\gamma=\frac{5}{\sqrt{17}}$$

$$\beta=\frac{\gamma\beta}{\gamma}$$

$$\beta=\frac{\sqrt{8}}{5}$$

$$v=\beta c$$

$$v\approx 1.7\times 10^{10} \unit{cm/s}$$

problem_statement:
Two accelerator facilities are under construction which will produce the neutral intermediate vector boson Z^0 via the process $$e^+ + e^- \to Z^0$$ The mass of the Z^0 is given by $$M_Z=92\unit{GeV}$$ Conventions and symbols: Natural units with c=1 are used unless a velocity is written explicitly with c. The electron mass is m_e and the muon mass is m_\mu. In the colliding-beam case, E denotes the beam energy per lepton in the laboratory, which coincides with the center-of-mass frame. In the fixed-target case, E_{e^+} and p_{e^+} are the laboratory energy and momentum of the incident positron, and the target electron is at rest. An overbar denotes a quantity in the center-of-mass (Z^0 rest) frame, for example \bar{E} and \bar{E}_\mu. The invariant mass squared of the initial state is S. The symbols \gamma_0 and \beta_0 are the Lorentz factor and speed (in units of c) of the center-of-mass frame relative to the laboratory. The symbols \gamma_\mu, \bar{\gamma}_\mu, and \bar{\beta}_\mu denote, respectively, the laboratory Lorentz factor of a decay muon and its Lorentz factor and speed in the Z^0 rest frame. The laboratory energy and speed of the produced Z^0 are E_Z and v_Z, and \beta_Z=v_Z/c.

a) Find the energy of the electron beam needed for the colliding beam facility under construction. Assume that a fixed target facility is to be built, such that a beam of e^+ will strike a target of e^- at rest.

b) What is the required e^+ beam energy for this case?

c) What is the energy and velocity of the Z^0 (in the laboratory) after production?

d) Find the maximum energy in the laboratory frame of muons from the subsequent decay Z^0 \to \mu^+ + \mu^-.
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 For the colliding-beam machine, the laboratory and center-of-mass frames coincide, so the threshold beam energy per lepton is $$E=\frac{M_Z}{2}$$ Using M_Z=92\unit{GeV}, this gives $$E=46\unit{GeV}$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 For the fixed-target facility, conservation of the invariant mass gives $$\left(E_{e^+}+m_e\right)^2-p_{e^+}^2=M_Z^2$$ Using the dispersion relation for the incident positron, $$E_{e^+}^2-p_{e^+}^2=m_e^2$$ we find the threshold energy $$E_{e^+}=\frac{M_Z^2-2 m_e^2}{2 m_e}$$ Neglecting the small term in m_e^2, $$E_{e^+}\approx\frac{M_Z^2}{2 m_e}$$ Numerically, $$E_{e^+}\approx 8.30\times 10^6\unit{GeV}$$

Solution for subproblem(c):
 Invariance of S gives $$S=\left(E_{e^+}+m_e\right)^2-p_{e^+}^2$$ and also $$S=\left(2\bar{E}\right)^2$$ Therefore, $$\bar{E}=\frac{\sqrt{2 m_e E_{e^+}+2 m_e^2}}{2}$$ At high energy, $$\bar{E}\approx\sqrt{\frac{m_e E_{e^+}}{2}}$$ At threshold, $$\bar{E}=\frac{M_Z}{2}$$ The Lorentz factor of the center-of-mass frame relative to the lab is $$\gamma_0=\frac{\bar{E}}{m_e}$$ Expressed in terms of laboratory quantities, $$\gamma_0=\sqrt{\frac{E_{e^+}}{2 m_e}+\frac{1}{2}}$$ At threshold, $$\gamma_0\approx\frac{M_Z}{2 m_e}$$ Since the Z^0 is produced at rest in the center-of-mass frame, its laboratory energy is $$E_Z=\gamma_0 M_Z$$ Hence, at threshold, $$E_Z\approx\frac{M_Z^2}{2 m_e}$$ and numerically $$E_Z\approx E_{e^+}$$ The corresponding speed parameter is $$\beta_Z=\sqrt{1-\frac{1}{\gamma_0^2}}$$ and the laboratory speed is $$v_Z=\beta_Z c$$ Using the threshold approximation, $$v_Z\approx\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{2 m_e}{M_Z}\right)^2} c$$ To first order, $$v_Z\approx\left(1-\frac{2 m_e^2}{M_Z^2}\right) c$$

Solution for subproblem(d):
 In the Z^0 rest frame, the decay is isotropic. Muons emitted in the direction of the incident e^+ have the maximum laboratory energy. In the center-of-mass frame, the Z^0 decays at rest into two muons, so $$\bar{E}_\mu=\frac{M_Z}{2}$$ and the corresponding Lorentz factor is $$\bar{\gamma}_\mu=\frac{\bar{E}_\mu}{m_\mu}$$ hence $$\bar{\gamma}_\mu=\frac{M_Z}{2 m_\mu}$$ For a muon moving along the boost direction, the inverse Lorentz transformation gives $$\gamma_\mu=\gamma_0\left(\bar{\gamma}_\mu+\beta_0\bar{\gamma}_\mu\bar{\beta}_\mu\right)$$ With \beta_0\approx\bar{\beta}_\mu\approx 1, $$\gamma_\mu\approx 2\gamma_0\bar{\gamma}_\mu$$ The maximum laboratory energy is $$E_{\mu,\max}=\gamma_\mu m_\mu$$ Hence, $$E_{\mu,\max}\approx 2\gamma_0\bar{\gamma}_\mu m_\mu$$ which evaluates to $$E_{\mu,\max}=\frac{M_Z^2}{2 m_e}$$ and therefore $$E_{\mu,\max}\approx E_{e^+}$$

The rho meson resonance of interest is the neutral rho, denoted rho^0, with rest mass m_rho = 769 MeV and decay width Gamma = 154 MeV. It can be produced experimentally by bombarding a hydrogen target with a pi^- meson beam via the reaction $$ \pi^- + p \to \rho^0 + n $$. Use the following conventions and constants throughout: m_pi = 140 MeV for the charged pion mass, m_p = 938 MeV for the proton mass, m_n = 940 MeV for the neutron mass, c = 3\times10^{10} \unit{cm/s} for the speed of light, and \hbar = 6.58\times10^{-22} \unit{MeV s} for the reduced Planck constant. In what follows, E_\rho denotes the laboratory energy of the produced rho^0, \tau_0 its proper lifetime, \tau its laboratory lifetime, and d its mean decay distance in the laboratory. The symbol S denotes the invariant mass squared of the system, E_\pi and p_\pi denote the energy and momentum of the incident pion, respectively, and \sigma, l, \rho, N_0, A denote the production cross section, target length, target density, Avogadro's number, and the target mass number, respectively. In part (d), quantities evaluated in the rho^0 rest frame \Sigma are denoted with an overbar, and \theta_{min} denotes the minimum opening angle between the outgoing pions in the laboratory frame.

a) What are the lifetime \tau and mean decay distance d for a rho^0 with laboratory energy E_\rho = 5 \unit{GeV}?

b) What is the pi^- threshold energy E_\pi for producing rho^0 mesons on a stationary proton target?

c) If the production cross section is \sigma = 1 \unit{mb} \equiv 10^{-27} \unit{cm^2} and the liquid hydrogen target is l = 30 \unit{cm} long, how many rho^0 are produced on average per incident pi^-? d) rho^0 mesons decay almost instantaneously into pi^+ + pi^-. Given that the rho^0 is produced in the forward direction in the laboratory frame with energy E_\rho = 5 \unit{GeV}, what is the minimum opening angle \theta_{min} between the outgoing pi^+ and pi^- in the laboratory frame?

Solution for subproblem(b):
 At threshold the invariant mass squared is $$ S = (E_\pi + m_p)^2 - p_\pi^2 $$ $$ S = (m_\rho + m_n)^2 $$ Using the on-shell condition for the incident pion, $$ E_\pi^2 = m_\pi^2 + p_\pi^2 $$ one obtains the threshold pion energy $$ E_\pi = \frac{(m_\rho + m_n)^2 - m_\pi^2 - m_p^2}{2 m_p} $$ Substituting numerical values gives $$ E_\pi = \frac{(769 \unit{MeV} + 940 \unit{MeV})^2 - (140 \unit{MeV})^2 - (938 \unit{MeV})^2}{2 \times 938 \unit{MeV}} $$ $$ E_\pi = 1077 \unit{MeV} $$

Solution for subproblem(c):

Solution for subproblem(d):
 In the rho^0 rest frame \Sigma, the two pions are back to back with equal energies $$ \bar E_\pi = \frac{m_\rho}{2} $$ The corresponding Lorentz factor for each pion in \Sigma is $$ \bar \gamma_\pi = \frac{\bar E_\pi}{m_\pi} $$ $$ \bar \gamma_\pi = \frac{m_\rho}{2 m_\pi} $$ The corresponding speed parameter is $$ \bar \beta_\pi = \sqrt{1 - \frac{1}{\bar \gamma_\pi^2}} $$ $$ \bar \beta_\pi = \frac{1}{m_\rho} \sqrt{m_\rho^2 - 4 m_\pi^2} $$ $$ \bar \beta_\pi = 0.93 $$ The rho^0 moves forward in the laboratory with $$ \gamma_0 = 6.50 $$ $$ \beta_0 = \sqrt{1 - \frac{1}{6.50^2}} $$ $$ \beta_0 = 0.99 $$ For pions emitted parallel and antiparallel to the rho^0 flight direction in \Sigma, both pions move forward in the laboratory because \beta_0 > \bar \beta_\pi, so the minimum opening angle is $$ \theta_{min} = 0 $$

a) Consider Compton scattering of photons that collide head-on with moving electrons, and observe back-scattered photons at scattering angle θ=180°. Let the incident photon energy be E_γ=hν=2\unit{eV}, where h is Planck's constant and ν is the photon frequency. The incident electron has kinetic energy T_e=1\unit{GeV}. Work in natural units with c=1, so the photon energy equals its momentum magnitude. Define the electron rest mass energy m_e=0.511\unit{MeV}. Denote the total energy and momentum magnitude of the incident electron by E_e and p_e, and those of the incident photon by E_γ and p_γ. After the collision, denote the corresponding quantities by E_e', p_e', E_γ', p_γ'. For photons E_γ=p_γ and E_γ'=p_γ'. Find the energy of the back-scattered photons, E_γ'.
reference_solution:
Conservation of energy gives
$$
E_\gamma+E_e=E_\gamma'+E_e'
$$
For photons
$$
E_\gamma=p_\gamma
$$
$$
E_\gamma'=p_\gamma'
$$
Conservation of momentum along the collision axis for a head-on collision with back-scattering gives
$$
-p_\gamma+p_e=p_\gamma'+p_e'
$$
Adding the previous two conservation equations gives
$$
E_e'+p_e'=-2p_\gamma'+E_e+p_e
$$
Subtracting the momentum equation from the energy equation gives
$$
E_e'-p_e'=2p_\gamma+E_e-p_e
$$
Multiplying the last two equations yields
$$
E_e'^2-p_e'^2=E_e^2-p_e^2+2p_\gamma(E_e+p_e)-2p_\gamma'(E_e-p_e+2p_\gamma)
$$
Using the on-shell conditions for the electron
$$
E_e'^2-p_e'^2=m_e^2
$$
$$
E_e^2-p_e^2=m_e^2
$$
Solving for the scattered photon momentum gives
$$
 p_\gamma'=\frac{p_\gamma(E_e+p_e)}{E_e-p_e+2p_\gamma}
$$
For an ultrarelativistic electron we use the approximations
$$
E_e-p_e=E_e-\sqrt{E_e^2-m_e^2}
$$
$$
\sqrt{E_e^2-m_e^2}\approx E_e\Big(1-\frac{m_e^2}{2E_e^2}\Big)
$$
$$
E_e-p_e\approx\frac{m_e^2}{2E_e}
$$
$$
E_e+p_e\approx 2E_e
$$
$$
E_e\approx T_e
$$
Substituting these into the expression for p_\gamma' gives
$$
 p_\gamma'\approx\frac{2p_\gamma E_e}{\frac{m_e^2}{2E_e}+2p_\gamma}
$$
Use the numerical values
$$
T_e=1\unit{GeV}
$$
$$
T_e=10^3\unit{MeV}
$$
$$
m_e=0.511\unit{MeV}
$$
$$
E_\gamma=2\unit{eV}
$$
$$
E_\gamma=2\times10^{-6}\unit{MeV}
$$
$$
p_\gamma=E_\gamma

$$

$$
Evaluating the expression gives
$$

$$

$$
E_\gamma'\approx29.7\unit{MeV}

The decay constant in the lab frame is

Time dilation gives

Solving for \gamma\beta,

T=\sqrt{\big(1.71\unit{GeV}\big)^2+\big(0.14\unit{GeV}\big)^2}-0.14\unit{GeV}

$$

problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) A particle of mass M=3\unit{GeV/c^2} moves along the x-axis in the laboratory with momentum p=4\unit{GeV/c}. It decays into two photons. In the parent-particle rest frame (denoted by overbars), the emission is isotropic: for the photon polar angle \theta^* measured from the x-axis in that frame, we have $$\frac{dP}{d\cos\theta^*}=\frac{1}{2}$$ Overbars, as in \bar E_i and \bar p_i for i=1,2, denote the energy and three-momentum of photon i in the parent-particle rest frame. Let p_x denote the x-component of a photon's momentum in the laboratory frame. Let \gamma be the Lorentz factor of the parent particle in the laboratory and \beta its speed in units of c in the laboratory. Define (p_x)_{max} and (p_x)_{min} as the maximum and minimum possible values of p_x, respectively. Determine (p_x)_{max} and (p_x)_{min}. Then find the probability density dP/dp_x as a function of p_x, and specify the domain on which it is valid.
reference_solution:
In the rest frame of the parent particle, conservation of energy and momentum gives
$$
\bar E_1+\bar E_2=M
$$
$$
\bar p_1+\bar p_2=0
$$
The photon momentum magnitudes are equal and opposite, and the photon energies are equal, so
$$
\bar p_1=\bar p
$$
$$
\bar p_2=\bar p
$$
$$
\bar E_1=\bar E
$$
$$
\bar E_2=\bar E
$$
Energy conservation then implies
$$
\bar E=\frac{M}{2}
$$
For photons in these units
$$
\bar p=\bar E
$$
With M=3\unit{GeV/c^2}
$$
\bar E=\frac{3}{2}\unit{GeV}
$$
$$
\bar p=\frac{3}{2}\unit{GeV/c}
$$
For the parent particle in the laboratory
$$
\gamma\beta=\frac{p}{M}
$$
$$
\gamma\beta=\frac{4}{3}
$$
$$
\gamma=\sqrt{(\gamma\beta)^2+1}
$$
$$
\gamma=\frac{5}{3}
$$
$$
\beta=\frac{\gamma\beta}{\gamma}
$$
$$
\beta=\frac{4}{5}
$$
The Lorentz transformation for the x component of a photon momentum gives
$$
 p_x=\gamma(\bar p\cos\theta^*+\beta\bar E)
$$
Using \bar p=\bar E
$$
 p_x=\gamma\bar p(\cos\theta^*+\beta)
$$
The maximum occurs at \theta^*=0, hence
$$
(p_x)_{max}=\gamma\bar p(1+\beta)
$$
$$
(p_x)_{max}=\frac{9}{2}\unit{GeV/c}
$$
The minimum occurs at \theta^*=\pi, hence
$$
(p_x)_{min}=\gamma\bar p(-1+\beta)
$$
$$
(p_x)_{min}=-\frac{1}{2}\unit{GeV/c}
$$
Differentiating the transformation relation gives
$$
 dp_x=\gamma\bar p\,d\cos\theta^*
$$
Therefore
$$
\frac{dP}{dp_x}=\frac{dP}{d\cos\theta^*}\frac{d\cos\theta^*}{dp_x}
$$
With isotropy in the rest frame
$$
\frac{dP}{dp_x}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{\gamma\bar p}
$$
Compute the factor
$$
\gamma\bar p=\frac{5}{2}\unit{GeV/c}
$$
Hence
$$
\frac{dP}{dp_x}=\frac{1}{5}\unit{c/GeV}
$$
This result holds on the support given by
$$
 p_x\ge (p_x)_{min}
$$
$$
 p_x\le (p_x)_{max}
$$

### Step 1: Parent boost

$$
\gamma=\sqrt{1+\frac{p^2}{M^2c^2}}
$$

$$
\gamma=\frac{5}{3}
$$

$$
\beta=\frac{p}{\gamma Mc}
$$

$$
\beta=\frac{4}{5}
$$

### Step 2: Photon momentum transformation

In the parent rest frame, each photon has energy $\bar E_i$ and momentum magnitude $|\bar p_i|$

$$
\bar E_i=\frac{Mc^2}{2}
$$

$$
|\bar p_i|=\frac{Mc}{2}
$$

$$

$$

A Lorentz boost along the \(x\)-axis gives

$$
p_x=\gamma\frac{Mc}{2}\left(\cos\theta^*+\beta\right)
$$

The extrema correspond to $\cos\theta^*=\pm1$

$$
(p_x)_{\max}=\gamma\frac{Mc}{2}(1+\beta)
$$

$$
(p_x)_{\max}=4.5\unit{GeV/c}
$$

$$
(p_x)_{\min}=\gamma\frac{Mc}{2}(\beta-1)
$$

$$
(p_x)_{\min}=-0.5\unit{GeV/c}
$$

### Step 3: Probability density

$$
\frac{dp_x}{d\cos\theta^*}=\frac{\gamma Mc}{2}
$$

Using $dP/d\cos\theta^*=1/2$

$$
\frac{dP}{dp_x}=\frac{dP}{d\cos\theta^*}\left|\frac{d\cos\theta^*}{dp_x}\right|
$$

$$
\frac{dP}{dp_x}=\frac{1}{\gamma Mc}
$$

$$
\frac{dP}{dp_x}=0.2\unit{c/GeV}
$$

This density is valid on

$$
-0.5\unit{GeV/c}\leq p_x\leq4.5\unit{GeV/c}
$$

Outside this interval

$$
\frac{dP}{dp_x}=0
$$

Since dp_x/dcosθ*=γMc/2 and dP/dcosθ*=1/2, dP/dp_x=1/(γMc)=0.2 c/GeV on that interval and zero outside; it also normalizes to 0.2×5=1.

problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) Consider the two-body decay K^0 -> pi^+ + pi^-. The transition matrix element is specified as T_{if} = [G / sqrt(8 E_K E_+ E_-)] [P_K (P_+ + P_-)] / m_K. Here E_K, E_+, and E_- are the relativistic energies of K^0, pi^+, and pi^- respectively, and P_K, P_+, and P_- are the corresponding four-momenta. The symbol P_A P_B denotes the Lorentz-invariant scalar product. The constants are: m_K for the K-meson mass, mu for the pion mass, G for the coupling constant, hbar for the reduced Planck constant, and c for the speed of light. In the rest frame of the decaying K^0, let p_1 and p_2 be the magnitudes of the three-momenta of pi^+ and pi^- respectively, E_1 and E_2 their energies (with E_1 = E_+ and E_2 = E_-), and Omega the solid angle. Let E denote the total final-state energy E = E_1 + E_2. The total transition probability per unit time is W, the density of final states is rho(E), and the lifetime measured in the K^0 rest frame is tau, with tau = 1/W. Assume the decay is isotropic. Show that the lifetime of the K^0 meson in its rest frame is tau = [ G^2 / (8 pi hbar^4 c) sqrt(m_K^2/4 - mu^2) ]^{-1}.
reference_solution:
The transition probability per unit time is
$$
W = \frac{2 \pi}{\hbar} |T_{if}|^2 \rho(E)
$$
In the K^0 rest frame,
$$
E_K = m_K c^2
$$
For a two-body decay into equal-mass pions,
$$
E_+ = \frac{1}{2} m_K c^2
$$
$$
E_- = \frac{1}{2} m_K c^2
$$
Four-momentum conservation gives
$$
P_K = P_+ + P_-
$$
Hence
$$
P_K^2 = m_K^2 c^2
$$
and
$$
(P_+ + P_-)^2 = P_K^2
$$
Therefore
$$
P_K (P_+ + P_-) = P_K^2
$$
The squared matrix element is
$$
|T_{if}|^2 = \frac{G^2}{8 E_K E_+ E_-} \frac{[P_K (P_+ + P_-)]^2}{m_K^2}
$$
Substituting the rest-frame relations yields
$$
|T_{if}|^2 = \frac{G^2}{2 m_K c^2}
$$
For a two-body decay in the parent rest frame, the density of final states is
$$
\rho(E) = \frac{1}{(2 \pi \hbar)^3} \frac{d}{dE} \int p_1^2 dp_1 d\Omega
$$
Assuming isotropy,
$$
\rho(E) = \frac{4 \pi}{(2 \pi \hbar)^3} \frac{d}{dE} \left( \frac{1}{3} p_1^3 \right)
$$
Momentum magnitudes satisfy
$$
p_1 dp_1 = p_2 dp_2
$$
The total energy differential is
$$
dE = dE_1 + dE_2
$$
Thus
$$
\frac{d}{dE} \left( \frac{1}{3} p_1^3 \right) = \frac{p_1^2 dp_1}{dE_1 + dE_2}
$$
Using the relativistic relation for each pion
$$
E_i^2 = p_i^2 c^2 + \mu^2 c^4
$$
we have
$$
\frac{dE_i}{p_i dp_i} = \frac{c^2}{E_i}
$$
Hence
$$
\frac{d}{dE} \left( \frac{1}{3} p_1^3 \right) = \frac{E_1 E_2 p_1}{c^2 (E_1 + E_2)}
$$
Therefore
$$
\rho(E) = \frac{4 \pi}{(2 \pi \hbar)^3} \frac{E_1 E_2 p_1}{c^2 (E_1 + E_2)}
$$
In the K^0 rest frame,
$$
E_1 = \frac{1}{2} m_K c^2
$$
$$
E_2 = \frac{1}{2} m_K c^2
$$
The pion three-momentum magnitude is
$$
 p_1 = c \sqrt{\frac{m_K^2}{4} - \mu^2}
$$
Thus
$$
\rho(E) = \frac{m_K c}{8 \pi^2 \hbar^3} \sqrt{\frac{m_K^2}{4} - \mu^2}
$$
Putting everything together,
$$
W = \frac{2 \pi}{\hbar} \frac{G^2}{2 m_K c^2} \frac{m_K c}{8 \pi^2 \hbar^3} \sqrt{\frac{m_K^2}{4} - \mu^2}
$$
Hence
$$
W = \frac{G^2}{8 \pi \hbar^4 c} \sqrt{\frac{m_K^2}{4} - \mu^2}
$$
The lifetime in the K^0 rest frame is
$$
\tau = W^{-1}
$$
Therefore
$$
\tau = \left[ \frac{G^2}{8 \pi \hbar^4 c} \sqrt{\frac{m_K^2}{4} - \mu^2} \right]^{-1}
$$
model_response:
### Solution

In the \(K^0\) rest frame, momentum conservation gives

$$
\boldsymbol p_1+\boldsymbol p_2=0
$$

Hence \(p_1=p_2=p\), and isotropy gives

$$
d^3p=p^2dpd\Omega
$$

$$
\int d\Omega=4\pi
$$

The pion energies are

$$
E_1=E_2=\sqrt{p^2c^2+\mu^2c^4}
$$

Energy conservation requires

$$
m_Kc^2=2\sqrt{p^2c^2+\mu^2c^4}
$$

Therefore

$$
p=c\sqrt{\frac{m_K^2}{4}-\mu^2}
$$

For the total final-state energy \(E=E_1+E_2\),

$$
\frac{dE}{dp}=\frac{2pc^2}{E_1}
$$

The density of final states is

$$
\rho(E)=\frac{4\pi p^2}{(2\pi\hbar)^3}\frac{dp}{dE}
$$

Thus, at \(E=m_Kc^2\),

$$
\rho(m_Kc^2)=\frac{m_Kp}{8\pi^2\hbar^3}
$$

Four-momentum conservation gives

$$
P_++P_-=P_K
$$

Consequently,

$$
P_K(P_++P_-)=m_K^2c^2
$$

Since \(E_K=m_Kc^2\),

$$
\lvert T_{if}\rvert^2=\frac{G^2m_Kc^2}{8E_1E_2}
$$

Using \(E_1=E_2=m_Kc^2/2\),

$$
\lvert T_{if}\rvert^2=\frac{G^2}{2m_Kc^2}
$$

Fermi’s golden rule gives

$$
W=\frac{2\pi}{\hbar}\lvert T_{if}\rvert^2\rho(m_Kc^2)
$$

Therefore

$$
W=\frac{G^2p}{8\pi\hbar^4c^2}
$$

Substituting the pion momentum,

$$
W=\frac{G^2}{8\pi\hbar^4c}\sqrt{\frac{m_K^2}{4}-\mu^2}
$$

Finally, \(\tau=1/W\), so

$$
\boxed{\tau=\left[\frac{G^2}{8\pi\hbar^4c}\sqrt{\frac{m_K^2}{4}-\mu^2}\right]^{-1}}
$$

Fast neutrons can be detected by observing scintillations caused by recoil protons in certain optically transparent hydrocarbons. Consider a slab of scintillator of thickness d=5\unit{cm} containing equal number densities n_H=n_C=4\times 10^{22}\unit{cm^{-3}} of hydrogen (H) and carbon (C) nuclei. A beam of neutrons of energy E_n\approx 5\unit{MeV} is incident normal to the slab. Let \sigma_H and \sigma_C denote the total interaction cross sections for neutrons on H and C, respectively, with 1\unit{barn}=10^{-24}\unit{cm^2}. Let N_0 be the number of neutrons incident on the entrance face, N(x) the number that have not interacted after traversing a depth x, and \eta=N(d)/N_0 the transmission fraction through the full thickness d. For part (b), define \eta'=1-\eta as the fraction that undergo at least one interaction in the slab, and let \eta'' be the fraction of incident neutrons that produce at least one recoil proton, assuming only interactions with H produce recoil protons.

a) What fraction of approximately 5\unit{MeV} neutrons incident normal to the slab will pass through the slab without interacting with either C or H nuclei?

b) What fraction of the incident neutrons will produce a recoil proton? Assume \sigma_H=\frac{3}{2}\unit{barn}, \sigma_C=1\unit{barn}, and 1\unit{barn}=10^{-24}\unit{cm^2}.
